Input: Haumiatiketike

Haumia-tiketike's stories are chapters of the Māori creation cycle: the separation of sky and earth, the war among the children, and the settlement of the food quest. His single decisive act is a refusal — to leave the earth-mother's body — and from that refusal the wild food of Aotearoa takes its sanctity. [Creation] Child of the Sky and the Earth: In the Māori creation cycle recorded by George Grey in Polynesian Mythology (1855) and in the fuller recensions of John White's Ancient History of the Māori , the sky-father Rangi and the earth-mother Papa lay locked in an embrace that left no room for light or life. Their children — Tāne, Tangaroa, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, Rongo-māui, Haumia-tiketike and the rest — grew cramped in the darkness between them. Among them Haumia was the quiet one, the god whose portion was to be everything the forest floor offered without planting. When at last the brothers voted on whether the parents should be separated, Haumia stood with Tāne: the world must be divided so that light, food, and people could come into it. The genealogy is short and absolute: every wild root dug in Aotearoa descends from this moment, when the children of the dark chose to break their parents' embrace and make room for a harvest. [The Separation] Hidden in the Earth-Mother: Tāne thrust his parents apart, raising the sky on his shoulders and pressing the earth down, and the world took its shape. But the separation left some children with nowhere to go. Tāwhirimātea, god of winds and storms, raged at what had been done and turned on his brothers; Tāne and Tangaroa fled to the forests and the sea. Rongo-māui took refuge inside the body of Papa, and Haumia-tiketike went with him — into the earth-mother's bosom, where the two brothers have remained ever since (Grey, Polynesian Mythology , 'The children of Heaven and Earth'). The story explains the Māori food world with an elegant symmetry: Rongo, who hid in the earth, is the god of the kūmara that must be planted; Haumia, who hid with him, is the god of the fernroot that is only gathered. What the mother shelters she does not surrender to the cultivator. [The War of the Brothers] The Food of the Conquered: When Tāwhirimātea's storms failed to unmake the world, Tūmatauenga — the fierce brother of humankind — took revenge on all who had sided against him. One by one he hunted his brothers down: Tāne's birds, Tangaroa's fish and seals, the very forests and waves were made food for Tū and his children, which is why people eat them to this day. But two brothers escaped him. Rongo and Haumia had hidden so deep within the body of Papa that no attack could reach them, and so Tū declared his sentence over them instead: because they dared not face him, they would be dug up — unearthed with the digging stick as the food of the conquered (Grey, 'The war of the children'; Orbell 1998). The myth gives uncultivated food its permanent rank in the Māori order: kūmara and fernroot are the flesh of gods who would not fight, and every meal of them replays the ancient war. [The Food Quest] Aruhe, the Fernroot: Haumia's living cult was the gathering of aruhe. From late winter into spring the people went out to the bracken clearings, dug the starchy rhizomes of the bracken fern with the foot-driven kō, and carried them home in baskets. The roots were beaten clean, washed in running water to leach the bitterness, and steamed for hours in the earth oven — hāngī, or umu tī, 'the fern oven'. When the kūmara crop failed, as it did in cold or wet years, aruhe carried whole communities through; Elsdon Best records that karakia were spoken over the digging, the cooking, and the first taste (Best, Māori Religion and Mythology ). In Haumia's domain there is no sowing and no fence: only the earth's own stores, opened by labor and gratitude. The god of wild food teaches that plenty does not always need a garden — it needs a country loved enough to be read.

Input: Svarog

Svarog has no surviving epic and no surviving cult — his entire dossier is a few chronicle lines, a gloss, and a name. The mythology below is therefore an archaeology of attestations: each 'myth' is a document, read as closely as the evidence allows, with the tradition's silence stated plainly. [The Book God] Named in the Izbornik of 1073: The earliest notice of Svarog comes not from a pagan shrine but from a court book. The Svyatoslav Izbornik of 1073 — a miscellany compiled for Prince Svyatoslav of Kiev — pauses over the Slavic gods to say: 'There is a god named Svarog' , and in the surrounding passage draws the comparison with the smith-god Hephaestus, whose forge was read as an image of heaven's fire. The compiler's source was probably a South Slavic manual translated for Duke Svyatoslav's court, which would make the notice the fossil of a lost Slavic mythographic handbook. The sentence is three words in Old Russian,The sentence is three words in Old Russian, yet it proves that in eleventh-century Rus', a century and a half after official conversion, learned men still needed to name and explain the old sky-smith. The attestation tells us less what Svarog did than how stubbornly he survived — a god preserved in the margin of a Christian book . [The Sun's Father] Svarog and the Birth of Dažbog: The Primary Chronicle (Povest' vremennykh let), in its anti-pagan sermon, records the genealogy plainly: 'from him was born Dažbog' — the Giving God, the sun — a line preserved in the Laurentian and Hypatian codices (Cross & Sherbowitz-Wetzor, trans.). Dažbog in turn gave his name to the Rus' themselves in the chronicler's bitter pun — 'Dažbog's grandchildren,' a folk memory the sermon meant to shame into silence. With it comes the whole logicWith it comes the whole logic of the sky-smith: what a smith fathers is a made light, a produced radiance, and Dažbog's very name ('the giver') reads like the boast of a successful forge. Scholars caution that the chronicler's sermon is polemic, not ethnography. Even so, the fragment preserves a genuine Indo-European intuition in Slavic dress: the sun is not a body but a work — hammered out, handed down, and called a gift . [The Western Witness] Zuarasici among the Slavic Gods: Writing around 1172, the German priest Helmold of Bosau lists the gods the Slavs revere — and among them, Zuarasici , the form his Latin ear gave to Svarog (Helmold, Chronica Slavorum I.52). The notice is a single name in a hostile catalogue, yet it matters: it places the god west of Kiev, among the Obodrite Slavs of the Baltic coast, suggesting his name once ranged across the whole Slavic world. The same passage gives him neighbors — a storm-hurling chief god and a god of war — so one hostile paragraph sketches the entire Obodrite pantheon. Helmold's list is our only Western-witness checkHelmold's list is our only Western-witness check on the Russian sources. A name without a story, recorded by an enemy, is fragile evidence — but it is evidence, and for a Slavic god that is rare enough to be precious . [The Little Svarog] Svarožič, Fire of the Hearth: In a Novgorod copy of Hilarion's Sermon on Law and Grace , a copyist 'corrected' the text to write Svarožič — 'Little Svarog' — the name scholars take for a fire-god or the domesticated form of the sky-smith (Ivanits, Russian Folk Belief , 1989; Gieysztor, Mitologia Słowian ). Later South Slavic and folk materials preserve hearth rites — the fire doused, fed, and addressed with honor — which the scholarship has long connected to this doubled name. South Slavic folklore collected in the nineteenth century still addresses the hearth fire with honorific formulas, and Serbian scholarship has long read in them the memory of a flame that was once a god. The tradition is fragmentary and the reconstruction debated;The tradition is fragmentary and the reconstruction debated; what stands is the shape of the idea: the cosmic smith had a small form that fit inside every house , so that tending the stove was, in origin, tending a god.

Tell me a myth about "Lada".

Input: Lada

No medieval Slavic text tells a myth of Lada . What survives is a trail of witnesses — a funeral play, a chronicler's glosses, Renaissance mythography, and living spring songs — from which scholarship must carefully separate memory from invention. Her 'mythology' is therefore the history of how a song-cry became a goddess, and an honest temple must tell it that way. [The Oldest Witness] The Refrain in the Round Dance: The oldest trace of Lada is not a story about her but a word sung in her place. In the spring round-dances of the South Slavs on Jurjevo — St George's Day, 6 May, when the grazing season opens — the cry Lado! punctuates the melody: greeting, praise, chorus, or the goddess herself, the sources never say. Young people cut the green oak, the zelenika , dance around it, and carry it to the pasture; nineteenth-century ethnographers among Croats, Serbs, and the Balkan Roma recorded the songs with the refrain intact. Farther north the same word softens into endearment: in Polish and Ukrainian wedding songs ladko and lado mean simply 'dear one.' The earliest stratum of the evidence is thus not narrative but music. If Lada was ever a full goddess, her first body was a song — which is why she has survived every empire that buried her chroniclers. [The School Play] Lada, Lel, and Polel on the Stage: The first text to list Lada among the gods is a joke at her expense. The Kraków school drama Pogrzeb świętej Roksany ('The Funeral of St. Roxane'), composed around 1500 and printed in 1535, brings together three students — a German, a Czech, and a Pole — to argue over whose hero deserves burial. The Pole defends his own ancestors: our gods, he insists, were Lada, Lel, and Polel , and our songs still remember them. The comedy mocks him for clinging to heathenry; but mockery preserves what reverence forgot, and the schoolboy's boast is now our earliest catalogue of Slavic divine names. The sources disagree even here: the play pairs Lada with Lel and Polel, while later writers split the twins differently and added genealogies no one attests. A goddess remembered in ridicule is still remembered — the play is less evidence of cult than of a name refusing, two centuries after conversion, to disappear. [The Chroniclers] The Glosses of Długosz and His Successors: Jan Długosz, the fifteenth-century Polish annalist, inserted into his Annales (Book I) marginal glosses on the old religion: the pagan Poles, he claims, used Lado for God himself, and among their goddesses he names Lada — glossing her, erratically, as Venus. The glosses, transmitted in the copy made by Stanisław Komasius, equate the native names so inconsistently that no modern scholar trusts the identifications. Later Renaissance mythography repeated and inflated them: Marcin Kromer's Polonia (1555), Maciej Stryjkowski's Kronika (1582) — which makes Lada a goddess of love — and Stanisław Sarnicki (1585) and Szymon Starowolski (1615), who repeat the lore with growing confidence. None of them cites a source older than folk memory. The chroniclers did not record Lada; they manufactured her — a caution this temple must carry at its threshold. [The Debate] Goddess or Refrain?: The nineteenth century decided the question by enthusiasm. Alexander Afanasyev's Poetic Views of the Slavs on Nature (1865–1869) enthroned Lada as a great goddess of spring and love, flanked by her twin sons Lel and Polel; Šafařík and Krek spread the picture across Slavdom, and Romantic art gave her a face. Twentieth-century scholarship pulled back hard: Michał Gieysztor's Mitologia Słowian (1982) keeps her cautiously, while Leszek P. Słupecki's Religia Słowian (2018) and other critics argue that the attestations are too late and too folkloric — that lado may never have been more than a refrain-word, with Lada its feminine form, like the wedding cry ladno still heard in Serbia. Comparatists set her beside the Greek Horai and the Latvian Laima, but no genetic link can be proven. The tradition is fragmentary and the sources openly disagree — and the debate itself, still alive, is the closest thing Lada has ever had to a cult.

Tell me a myth about "Ītzpāpālōtl".

Input: Ītzpāpālōtl

Itzpapālōtl belongs to the dangerous borderlands: between paradise and underworld, birth and death, daylight and eclipse. Her myths are preserved in fragments of the Florentine Codex, the Borgia-group codices, and late alphabetic histories — and where the evidence is late, the entry says so. [Origin] The Lady of Tamoanchan: Tamoanchan is the paradise of origins in Nahua thought — a lush mountain of flowers beyond the human world, where the gods dwelt and where humanity was fashioned (López Austin, Tamoanchan, Tlalocan ). Itzpapālōtl rules there as guardian and terror at once: in the codices she appears with obsidian-bladed wings and taloned jaguar claws, mistress of a beauty that cuts the hand that touches it. The Florentine Codex treats her as one of the formidable powers of the upper world, and the name itself — ītztli , 'obsidian', joined to papālōtl , 'butterfly' (Karttunen, An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl ) — is a theological statement: the loveliest thing in the air, built from the sharpest thing in the earth. In her, paradise and its danger are one flower. [Migration] The Butterfly Who Led the Chichimecs: Later alphabetic sources attach Itzpapālōtl to the Chichimec ancestors of the Mexica. The Historia de los Mexicanos por sus pinturas (c. 1540) names an obsidian butterfly among the wonder-beings of the migration age, and the Anales de Cuauhtitlan preserves the wider lore of the Chichimecs' star-guided wanderings out of Chicomoztoc, the Seven Caves. The evidence is late and fragmentary — friars wrote down what their informants said, and the Borgia-group codices show her sign without narrating her story — so the tradition should be cited with caution. But the association fits her astronomy: a people guided through the dark north by a star-demon. She is migration itself made divine — fragile as a butterfly, cutting as flint, leading the nameless toward an empire. [Childbirth] Mother of the Cihuateteo: Women who died in childbirth did not become ordinary dead. They became Cihuateteo, 'divine women' — fierce spirits who accompanied the sun from its zenith to the western horizon and descended at crossroads to threaten the living (Florentine Codex; Karttunen, s.v. cihuateotl). Itzpapālōtl is their mother and queen. The midwife's orations preserved in the Florentine Codex address the dead woman as a warrior fallen in battle, honoured like a slain captive: she had died, the texts say, capturing a child for the people. The theology is exact — childbirth was a war, the lying-in room a battlefield, and its queen a butterfly whose wings were blades. The myth dignifies a death no weapon caused, and reads maternity as the risk that wins. [Astronomy] The Black Butterfly of Eclipse: As a Tzitzimitl, Itzpapālōtl belongs to the star-demons of the northern sky — skeletal women, powers of the dark, who descend when the cosmic order fails (Seler's commentary on the Borgia group; Florentine Codex). During an eclipse the Nahua believed the Tzitzimime descended head-first to devour the sun or the moon, and the people answered with noise, raised weapons, and blood offerings until the light returned. Itzpapālōtl is the most terrible among them: the eclipse made personal, a black butterfly settling on the world's lamp. The rite is the meaning — chaos is fought not only with armies but with the gathered din of an entire people, terror communal answered communally, the way a whole village shouts at the dark until it lifts.

Tell me a myth about "Tlāltēcuhtli".

Input: Tlāltēcuhtli

Tlāltēcuhtli appears in several Mesoamerican creation accounts as the earth monster who must be defeated and dismembered before the present world can exist. The most detailed Nahuatl version survives in the Histoyre du Méchique , a sixteenth-century colonial manuscript; the Leyenda de los Soles and the Florentine Codex supply parallel doctrines. These sources are fragmentary and written after the conquest — the tradition itself says so, and this temple reports them as such. [Creation myth] The Dismemberment of the Earth Monster: Our fullest Nahua creation account survives in a sixteenth-century French manuscript, the Histoyre du Méchique (associated with the cosmographer André Thevet) — colonial, fragmentary, and precious for exactly that reason. It tells that the gods Quetzalcōātl and Tēzcatlīpōca, seeing a great monster in the form of a caiman called Tlāltēcuhtli floating on the primordial waters, transformed themselves into two great serpents and seized her, one by the right hand and foot, one by the left, and tore her in two. From one half they made the earth, from the other the sky; from her hair they made trees, plants, and flowers, from her eyes wells and springs, from her nose rivers and valleys, from her shoulders mountains. The victim did not die quietly: she cried out in the night for the hearts of men, and the gods consented to feed her. The Leyenda de los Soles tells a parallel creation. The myth's meaning is contract, not conquest: the world exists because a being was broken, and it keeps existing only while the debt of flesh is paid. [Solar myth] The Sun's Nightly Journey: The Florentine Codex — the encyclopedia compiled under Bernardino de Sahagún from Nahua elders in the 1540s–1570s — describes the sun's nightly passage in the plainest physical terms: at evening the sun enters the gaping mouth of the earth in the west, passes through the body of Tlāltēcuhtli, and is delivered again at dawn in the east. To the sources this is no metaphor: the earth has a mouth, jaws, and hunger, and the day itself is a meal it cannot be allowed to refuse. Nahuatl vocabulary underwrites the image — the earth is tlālli , and Tlāltēcuhtli is that land made lord. The doctrine that night is the sun passing through a body made every evening an act of digestion and every morning a birth: in this cosmology time does not flow above the world but through it, and the calendar keeps its count in the gut of the ground. [Ritual foundation] Offerings to the Hungry Earth: Sahagún's informants describe a relationship of payment. Before a house was built, a field planted, or a body buried, the earth was addressed and fed — food, flowers, copal incense, and in the highest rites blood — because unfed earth refuses its function (Florentine Codex, Books 1 and 11; Durán, Book of the Gods and Rites ). The Codex Magliabechiano illustrates precisely such offerings set before a crouching earth figure. The archaeological correlate is overwhelming: the Templo Mayor excavations have recovered dedicatory caches buried as gifts to the earth at every stage of construction, some containing the remains of sacrifice. Colonial friars read this as devil-worship; the Nahua informants present it as ordinary courtesy. Both testify to the same theology: the ground under Mexico City was never inert — it was a creditor holding the mortgage on every foundation stone. [Modern discovery] The Red Monolith Beneath the Cathedral: On 2 October 2006, in a trench at the foot of the Templo Mayor, Leonardo López Luján's team uncovered a slab that made international news: a monolithic Tlāltēcuhtli more than four metres across, carved crouching with claws extended, a skull at the waist-buckle, death's eyes in its sockets, and traces of red and yellow pigment still in the stone. López Luján associated the monument with the nearby cremation deposits of Mexica rulers — above all Ahuitzotl, who died in 1502 — reading it as the earth lord summoned to receive a king. The find completed a five-hundred-year symmetry: the colonial city was built over the earth's face, its cathedral stones cut from the temples of the precinct; the excavation put the face back into the light. The earth, the Aztecs said, always gets what it is owed — even if payment comes in the currency of archaeology, and five centuries late.

Tell me a myth about "Ọrúnmìlà".

Input: Ọrúnmìlà

Ọrúnmìlà's mythology lives in the thousands of Ifá verses (òdù Ifá) that record his journeys, judgments, and interventions — wisdom's biography told as scripture. [Cosmogony] The Witness at the Foundation of the World: According to Ifá tradition, Ọrúnmìlà was the only orixá present when Olódùmarè created the earth. He observed the placing of the rivers, the rising of the mountains, and the distribution of destinies, and the corpus never stops drawing authority from that attendance (Abimbola, Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus , 1976; Bascom, Ifa Divination , 1969). The other orishas received domains; Ọrúnmìlà received the memory of everything. Because he witnessed the beginning, he can trace any present trouble back to its origin and prescribe the sacrifice that will set it right. The Ifá verses return to this scene whenever authority is questioned, and it has silenced sceptics for centuries. The myth defines knowledge as witnessing rather than power: the one who watched the world being made became the one to whom the world turns when it forgets what it is for. [Origin] Àgbọnnìrègún, the Medicine That Never Fails: Before descending to earth, Ọrúnmìlà received from Olódùmarè the gift called àgbọnnìrègún — the sixteen sacred palm nuts and the science of reading them, glossed in the corpus as 'the medicine that never fails' (Bascom 1969; Idowu, 1962). The myth has a practical moral: the other orishas came down with powers over fire, water, and iron, but Ọrúnmìlà came down with a method. Wherever he travelled — and the verses send him wandering through every kind of settlement — he could answer any question put to him by casting the nuts and reciting the odù that fell. That is why the nuts are addressed with the respect due a founder, and why their loss ends a priest's career. The story makes divination a deliberate endowment, not an improvisation: heaven equipped its witness with the one tool the world would never stop needing. [Destiny] The Man Who Chose a Bad Head: A celebrated òdù narrative tells of a man who, before birth, knelt impatiently in heaven and seized the first head Àjàlá the potter offered — a cracked, ill-fired orí. On earth his life collapsed: his farms failed, his wives left, his name soured. At last he consulted Ifá, performed the prescribed sacrifice, and in a dream journey returned to the house of Àjàlá, where he exchanged the ruined head for a sound one; he woke on earth a different man (Abimbola 1976; the Orí cycle of narratives). The story is the corpus's most beloved parable of hope: destiny chosen cannot be unchosen, but heaven keeps a pottery, and sacrifice is the road back to it. Ọrúnmìlà's role is never to mock the careless chooser — only to chart the road back. [Counsel] The Client Who Would Not Sacrifice: Countless òdù verses end the same way: a person consults Ifá, receives a precise prescription — offer this, avoid that — and ignores it; ruin follows exactly as the odù said it would (Bascom 1969 catalogues the motif). Sometimes the refuser is a king who will not humble himself, sometimes a trader who counts the ẹbọ too dear. Ọrúnmìlà never punishes; the ignored counsel simply unfolds, the way an unread letter still contains its bad news. The motif is the corpus's pedagogy of practice: divination is not knowledge for its own sake but knowledge tied to an act. A verse unperformed is a door left shut, and a sacrifice owed is a debt the world always collects. The god of wisdom measures understanding the way a doctor measures recovery — not by what you heard, but by what you did.

Tell me a myth about "Altjira".

Input: Altjira

The mythology of Altjira comes to us through Arrernte oral tradition and the early ethnographies of Spencer and Gillen, Carl Strehlow, and later scholars. The stories are not entertainment; they are title deeds to country, instructions for ceremony, and maps of moral responsibility. Some details are held by initiated custodians and are not shared in public space. [Arrernte cosmogony] The Uncreated Creator: In the account recorded by Spencer and Gillen, Altjira is eternal: he was not born and will not die. In the beginning he made the earth and all that it contains — its hills, waterholes, plants, and animals — and then he rose into the sky, where he remains with his two sons. The earth was left for the ancestors who followed and for the human beings who would inherit their law (Spencer & Gillen, The Arunta , 1927; Carl Strehlow, Die Aranda- und Loritja-Stämme ). Later Arrernte teaching, above all T. G. H. Strehlow's, corrected the early picture: altjira is less a person than the eternal order itself. The word thus carries its own commentary — creator and creation-principle named alike, as if the language insisted that the maker cannot be separated from what making means. [Arrernte cosmogony] The Sky Above: Altjira lives in the sky, high above the camps of men and women. His feet are like the feet of the emu, and he never bends them, because the sky is wide and there is no obstacle in his path. The stars and the Milky Way are the camps and tracks of ancestral beings, so that the night sky is read as a mirror of the country below (Spencer & Gillen; Berndt & Berndt, The World of the First Australians ). The detail is characteristically Australian: a creator imagined not enthroned but walking — a sky roomy enough that the eternal being in it never has to stoop. Here creation is not a pyramid with a god on top but a landscape with a footpath, and the footpath belongs to something older than the walker's arrival. [The Dreaming] Alcheringa: The term alcheringa — rendered from Arrernte altjira — names the Dreaming: the time when the ancestors moved across the land, creating its forms and leaving behind the songs, designs, and ceremonies that maintain it. Altjira is both the name of the eternal sky being and the name of the epoch in which the world received its present shape. Later Arrernte scholarship, especially T. G. H. Strehlow's Aranda Traditions (1947), stressed that altjira primarily means 'to dream' and refers to the eternal creative order rather than to a single personal deity comparable to the biblical God. The ambiguity is the doctrine: in Arrernte thought the dream and the order it discloses are one word, and a vocabulary that separates god from epoch is translating something that was never divided. [Living tradition] Custodianship: The public, scholarly record of Altjira is only one layer of knowledge. Arrernte custodians hold song-cycles, designs, and ceremonial responsibilities that are not published and are transmitted under strict traditional protocols. PuniCodex presents only the documented, open scholarly account and acknowledges that deeper knowledge belongs to the communities who keep it. The restraint is itself part of the mythology: a tradition whose deepest layer is protected teaches, by its silence, what sacredness is — that some knowledge is not secret because it is threatened, but powerful because it is withheld, and that the shoreline of the public record is not the edge of the sea.

Tell me a myth about "Yurlungur".

Input: Yurlungur

The central Yurlungur myth is an initiation narrative: a boy breaks a food prohibition, is swallowed by the great copper python, and is restored to his kin only after the correct ritual response. In that single event the whole logic of Yolŋu male initiation — death to childhood, passage through the ancestor's body, rebirth as a man — is enacted for the first time. The early ethnographies differ in detail, even in the serpent's gender; the myths below follow the common structure. [Murngin] The Swallowing of Wawi: At the first borum ceremony, the boy Wawi ate food that had been forbidden to him — and the great copper python, sleeping in the deep waterhole, heard the law being broken. Yurlungur rose, traveled through the earth to where the people were camped, and swallowed the boy whole . The ancestors were dismayed; the ceremony could not continue with the law's transgression unexpired. The boy's mother followed his tracks to the edge of the sacred pool, the place where the human world opens into the ancestral realm, and there she wept and sang. Moved — or shamed — by her grief, the python vomited the boy out , alive but no longer a child. From that day the pattern was set: every novice must enter the ancestral body and emerge again. Initiation is, in the myth's own terms, a controlled swallowing: the boy dies into the snake and is reborn as a man. [Murngin] The Mother at the Waterhole: The mother's pursuit is as important as the snake's swallowing. She traces Wawi to the rim of the sacred pool and there does the one thing the law cannot do without her: she mourns correctly — weeping, singing, calling the ancestor by the obligations it owes her line. The ethnographers who recorded the cycle in the 1920s and 1930s (Warner, then the Berndts) heard in this scene the partnership of male and female knowledge in initiation: the men own the rite, the bullroarer, and the enclosure, but the relational power that compels the ancestor to give the child back belongs to the mother and her kin. The story thus encodes more than a punishment. It maps the division of religious labor that holds Yolŋu society together — the law swallows; the kinship system gives back — and it makes the waterhole, where the two worlds touch, the most dangerous and most necessary place in the country. [Murngin] The First Borum Ground: After Wawi's return, the ground around Yurlungur's waterhole became the prototype of the borum ground — the cleared ceremonial space where, in every generation since, novices are separated from women and children, painted with white ochre, shown the sacred objects of adulthood, and made to hear the bullroarer's voice, which is the serpent's own. The myth supplies the architecture: a dangerous perimeter, an ancestral interior, a transformation that cannot be undone. The novices who enter the enclosure are told, in the old men's instruction, that they too have been inside the great snake; the pain and fear of the rite are the memory of its body. A borum is therefore not an imitation of the myth but its repetition — the first swallowing carried forward, boy by boy, so that the ancestor's act at the beginning remains alive at every beginning since. [Comparative] Rainbow Serpent Typology: Yurlungur belongs to the Rainbow Serpent family that stretches across Aboriginal Australia — Ngalyod in western Arnhem Land, the Waugal of the southwest, Wanambi in the central deserts, and dozens of locally owned names beside. Like them he links water, fertility, and ancestral law; like them he punishes the breaking of taboo and rewards the keeping of it with rain and children. But the comparative label can mislead. 'Rainbow Serpent' is an English scholarly convenience, not an Aboriginal category, and the regional figures differ sharply: Yurlungur is specifically tied to male initiation and to the copper-coloured python that gives him his name, while Berndt's Kunapipi materials make the cognate serpent Yulunggur a female mother-ancestor of a different rite. The honest summary is that Australia does not have one rainbow snake but hundreds of owned, local ancestors who share a grammar — water, law, danger, and the crossing between worlds .

Tell me a myth about "Anima".

Input: Anima

Anima is not a mythological character in the Greek or Roman sense; it is a concept that acquired a long philosophical and theological history. Its 'mythology' is therefore the story of how breath became soul, and how soul became one of the foundation stones of Western psychology. [Roman thought] The Breath of Life: In Classical Latin anima first names the air itself: the breeze in the trees, the breath in the lungs. Cicero uses the word for the vital spirit that ties soul to body ( Tusculanae disputationes 1), but the word's great theorist is the materialist Lucretius. In De rerum natura 3 he argues that the soul is a bodily thing — a subtle compound of heat, air, and wind, fine as smoke — dispersed and destroyed when the body dies. To understand the soul correctly, for Lucretius, is to be cured of the fear of death: no afterlife, no punishment, only rest. The Latin word thus begins as physiology and becomes philosophy in a single step. Western psychology starts here — not with a ghost in a machine, but with weather inside the body, measurable in warmth and breath. [Christian theology] The Rational Soul: Early Latin Christianity adopted anima as the standard rendering of Greek psychē , and the word's career turned theological. Tertullian devoted a treatise to it ( De anima ); Augustine's De quantitate animae asks, in dialogue, what the soul's 'magnitude' can be; Boethius made the soul the hinge of the Consolation of Philosophy . The scholastics completed the fusion: following Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas calls the soul the body's form — 'the first principle of life in things which live in our world' ( Summa Theologiae I.75.1) — and the Council of Vienne (1312) defined as doctrine that the rational soul is truly, of itself, the form of the human body. The breath-word ended up carrying the heaviest load in Christian metaphysics, while never quite losing its breeze: between clinic and creed, anima kept both meanings at once. [Modern psychology] Jung's Anima: In C. G. Jung's analytical psychology the anima is the unconscious feminine image carried within a man's psyche — the animus its masculine counterpart in a woman. She is the soul-figure who appears in dreams, projects onto living women, mediates between the ego and the deep unconscious, and — in Jung's phrase — is 'the archetype of life itself' ( Aion , CW 9ii). His early formulation ( The Relations between the Ego and the Unconscious , 1928) treats her as the very function through which a man experiences his own soul. The ancient equation survives intact under the new terminology: the soul is still made of air, but now the air is what moves between two people — the atmosphere of feeling and relationship that modern psychology learned to study by giving it her old Latin name. [Modern language] Animation and Life: The descendants of anima form a genealogy of the living. An animal is a being that breathes; to animate is to put breath into matter; animation is the craft of giving apparent life to drawings; animism is the ascription of soul to rivers, trees, and stones; equanimity is an even soul; unanimity is many spirits agreeing as one. Each English word preserves a different inflection of the Latin root, and each still points back to breath. Two thousand years after Lucretius dispersed the soul into wind, every cartoon that moves, every creature that breathes, and every argument that matter itself might be alive still testifies to the old insight the word was coined to hold: that the difference between living and dead is the presence of something as invisible, and as real, as air.

Tell me a myth about "Bāguà".

Input: Bāguà

The Bāguà are surrounded by origin stories that credit culture heroes and sages with their discovery. Fuxi reads the patterns of the world; King Wen elaborates the Changes in a Shang prison; the sages of the Xici invent the book as they invented writing and agriculture — in answer to human need. Whether history, legend, or mythic shorthand, the stories agree on one thing: the eight trigrams are a key to cosmic order, perfected at great cost. [Xici Tradition] Fuxi Reads the Patterns of the World: The oldest account of the trigrams' invention is not a story about a river monster but a sentence in the Xici zhuan (Appended Statements II): 'In ancient times, when Bao Xi (Fuxi) ruled the world, he looked up and contemplated the patterns of heaven, looked down and contemplated the patterns of earth; he observed the markings of birds and beasts and the adaptations of the land. Near at hand he took patterns from his own body, far off he took them from things — and so he created the eight trigrams to communicate with the virtue of the gods and to categorize the feelings of all things.' Later legend embroidered the contemplation into a marvel: a dragon-horse emerged from the Yellow River bearing the Hétú chart, and a divine turtle from the Luo bore the Luoshu writing, and from these the sage read the trigrams. The tradition itself (Xici I) preserves the kernel: 'The river produced the chart, the Luo produced the document; the sage modelled himself on them.' Either way, the claim is identical: the trigrams were not invented but noticed — the cosmos already written, waiting only to be read. [Shiji Tradition] King Wen Elaborates the Changes in Prison: When King Wen of Zhou was imprisoned by the tyrant Zhòu of Shang — the tradition recorded by Sima Qian — he did not plot escape but divination: 'King Wen was imprisoned and elaborated the Zhōuyì ' (Shiji 130). In captivity he doubled the eight trigrams into sixty-four hexagrams and wrote a statement for each, a one-line oracle distilled from the history and ethics of a people living under an oppressive dynasty. His son, the Duke of Zhou, is credited with the line statements, the judgements within each hexagram; Confucius or his school, centuries later, added the Ten Wings, turning a manual of milfoil divination into a philosophy of change. Sima Qian's sentence has carried enormous weight: it makes the Yijing literally a prison book, written by a condemned man mapping the one freedom no cell can close — the freedom to read the moment. The sequence of authorship — king, duke, sage — also quietly encodes the book's social range: ruler, minister, teacher. [Xici] The Sage Who Invents According to Need: The Xici appendix imagines human technology not as a fall but as a series of sages answering crises. When rule by knotted cords became inadequate, a later sage replaced them with written characters; before that, another sage taught agriculture when birds and beasts dwindled under bad kings. In the same passage, the author explains the Yijing 's purpose: the sages made the eight trigrams and 'exposed the auspicious and inauspicious in them,' so that the people could meet each situation as it arose. Change ( yi ) is the one constant; the book exists because human beings need a grammar for situations that have never occurred before. This is why the Yijing never gives straight predictions — it gives structures for reflection. The myth of sage-invention dignifies the diviner: to consult the book is to join a long chain of sage problem-solvers, from Fuxi, who fished and hunted, through Shennong, who sowed, to King Wen, who suffered and saw. [Folk Religion] The Bagua Mirror Guards the Door: In Chinese popular religion the eight trigrams descend from the scholar's desk to the lintel. The bāguà jìng — an octagonal mirror ringed with the trigrams around a taiji emblem at its centre — is hung above doorways across China and the diaspora to deflect harmful qi . A flat mirror confronts what comes straight; a concave mirror gathers and neutralizes; a convex mirror scatters 'poison arrows' from rooflines, sharp corners, and aggressive neighbours. Priests of the Daoist liturgical tradition also deploy the trigrams spatially: ritual registers assign each trigram a direction and a gate, and the complete octagonal arrangement claims the whole of space and time in a single emblem. The practice compresses the entire cosmology into household hardware — heaven, earth, thunder, wind, water, fire, mountain, and lake standing sentinel over a family's doorway. Whatever else it does, the mirror announces that the cosmos has a shape, and that a household can align itself with it.

Tell me a myth about "Wꜣḏyt".

Input: Wꜣḏyt

Wadjet's mythology is woven into kingship from the first dynasties, present more as an institution than a protagonist. She has no single epic cycle; she has a thousand crowns, amulets, and royal names — and her stories cluster around four poles: the Two Ladies, the divine child, the wandering Eye, and the Delta oracle at Buto. [Kingship] The Two Ladies: From the unification of the Two Lands, the cobra stood beside the vulture over every royal name: Wadjet of the Delta and Nekhbet of Elkab together were the nbty , the Two Ladies, and their pairing was the political theology of Egypt — two lands, two crowns, one body wearing both. On the Narmer Palette (Cairo JE 32169), the king of the First Dynasty already processes beneath the standards of his protectors, and the serekhs of his successors frame the royal name with the two beasts. By the reign of King Den the pair had entered the titulary itself as the title nbty , 'He of the Two Ladies' — the first element of the fivefold royal protocol. Every coronation oath for three thousand years was thus sworn in her presence, on the brow. The myth is a constitution written as heraldry: sovereignty is legitimate only when north and south, vulture and cobra, consent to share a single head. [Divine Child] Nurse of the Divine Child: In the Delta marshes, when Isis hid the infant Horus from Seth among the papyrus thickets of Chemmis, the snakes of the goddess stood guard. Wadjet is the serpent of the thicket — hood spread over the nursing god, flame ready for any scavenging demon. The protection was theologically exact: Horus was the king, so the Delta goddess guarded in myth what her uraeus guarded in fact, the brow of every living pharaoh, 'the nursling of Wadjet'. The scene's most beloved monument is the Metternich Stela and its kin, the Horus cippi of the Late Period (c. 360 BCE): on them the child-god, stung by scorpions in the reeds, is healed by his mother while the surrounding deities — Wadjet among them — contract to shield the cippi's owner from every crawling thing. The myth taught an Egyptian peasant of any century the same lesson the crown taught the court: in the reeds, as on the throne, survival depends on a serpent who has chosen you. [The Eye of Re] The Distant Goddess Returns: Like Sekhmet, Tefnut, and Hathor, Wadjet can act as the solar Eye that departs in rage and must be coaxed home. The cycle is set out in the great commentaries on Book of the Dead spell 17: the Eye of Horus is struck down and scattered — by Seth in one telling — and Thoth gathers and restores it, the sound, whole, 'wedjat' eye; restored, it burns from the king's brow as the uraeus, the healed eye that has become a weapon. When the Eye wanders far south as the Distant Goddess, the land withers; when it returns, the Delta greens. For Wadjet the return is literal: her name means 'the green one', and her homecoming is the inundation's fresh silt spreading over the fields. The theology binds protection to growth in a single image: the same eye that was broken and made whole now makes the land whole, and the cobra on the crown is the scar tissue of the cosmos — injury, restored, promoted to sentry. [Temple] Buto and the Oracle: Her ancient cult center was Pe-Dep — the twin towns of Pe and Dep in the western Delta, Greek Buto — where she was worshipped in a temple famed as an oracle; Herodotus (2.59) counts Buto among Egypt's great oracular shrines, and (2.63) describes its sanctuary with the respect he reserves for the old and uncanny. There, in the reeds of the deepest Delta, Egyptian theology placed the primordial mound where creation began and where Isis nursed Horus — Buto was the wet nurse of the world. Greek visitors, hearing that this goddess guarded a divine child in a marsh, identified her city with Leto , mother of Apollo and Artemis, two other children hidden in reeds — an interpretatio the sources themselves found almost too neat. Excavations at Tell el-Fara'in have uncovered the temple's Late Period and Ptolemaic remains above occupation layers reaching back into prehistory, confirming what the priests always claimed: Buto was old before Egypt had a name for old.

Tell me a myth about "Manawydan".

Input: Manawydan

Manawydan's dossier is the Second and Third Branches of the Mabinogi: Branwen ferch Llŷr, where he is one of the seven who bring the head home, and Manawydan fab Llŷr, the branch that bears his name — the quietest and most perfectly built of the Four, a tale in which an entire kingdom is stolen by silence and won back by patience. [Second Branch · Branwen ferch Llŷr] The Seven Who Brought the Head Home: Manawydan stands beside his brother Brân — Bendigeidfran, the Blessed — when [[matholwch|Matholwch]], king of Ireland, comes to Harlech to ask for their sister Branwen, and he counsels the marriage that begins the whole catastrophe. When the insult of the mutilated horses has festered into war, Brân wades the sea to Ireland, and the host that crosses with him comes home as seven men: Pryderi, Manawydan, Glifieu Eil Taran, [[taliesin|Taliesin]], Ynawg, Gruddieu fab Muriel, and Heilyn fab Gwyn — bearing the head of Brân, struck by a poisoned spear, which talks with them and is better company than ever it was in life. At Harlech they feast seven years with the head, the three songs of the birds of Rhiannon singing to them, and time does not move. At Gwales in Penfro they find a royal hall with two doors open and one shut — toward Cornwall — and there they pass eighty years in the Assembly of the Wondrous Head, forgetting every sorrow, until Heilyn fab Gwyn says 'shame on my beard if I do not open the door' — and opens it, and all their losses come back at once like a tide. Then they do as the head had commanded: they carry it to London and bury it in the White Mount, facing France, and the triads count that burial among the Three Fortunate Concealments of the Island of Britain. Manawydan, who had counseled the wedding, survives its end — the pattern of his whole life in one branch. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The Counsel and the Marriage: While Brân's host was in Ireland, Caswallawn fab [[beli|Beli]] — Manawydan's own cousin — had struck down the men left in charge and taken the crown of London. Pryderi, lord of Dyfed and son of Pwyll and [[rhiannon|Rhiannon]], would have fought him; Manawydan counsels otherwise: Caswallawn is their kinsman, and the kingdom has suffered enough of war. It is the most characteristic speech in the whole Mabinogi — a man with the best claim to vengeance declining it out of arithmetic and mercy. Pryderi yields, and gives Manawydan the fairest compensation the tale can imagine: his mother's hand and the seven cantrefs of Dyfed. Manawydan and Rhiannon wed, and the four — Manawydan, Rhiannon, Pryderi, and Pryderi's wife Cigfa — live at Arberth in unbroken fellowship. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The Thunder and the Mist: They go up Gorsedd Arberth, the mound where, in the First Branch, wonders came to Pwyll — and wonder comes. As they sit, a peal of thunder falls, and with it a mist so thick they cannot see one another. When it lifts, Dyfed is gone: no dwelling, no animal, no smoke, no man, no woman — only the four of them and the empty land, house and court and courtiers vanished together. For a year they live by hunting and the kindness of the emptied land; for a second year they bear it; in the third they grow weary of it, and the tale turns from endurance to answer. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The White Boar and the Golden Bowl: Hunting, Pryderi and Manawydan rouse a boar shining white, which leads their dogs to a fortress neither has ever seen — and no one ever sees twice. Against Manawydan's counsel Pryderi goes in after the dogs and finds a fountain with a marble slab, and on the slab a golden bowl fastened by chains, wrought with a craftsmanship he cannot fathom. He reaches for it: his hands stick to the bowl, his feet to the slab, and speech leaves him. Rhiannon, hearing her son lost, reproaches Manawydan for returning without him, goes in, lays hold of the bowl, and is taken the same way — and with thunder and a fall of mist the fortress vanishes with them both. Manawydan is left with Cigfa, and the branch's second act belongs to them alone. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The Three Crafts of Hereford: Manawydan will not beg his bread in an emptied kingdom: 'Let us go into Lloegr,' he tells Cigfa, 'and take up a craft.' At Hereford he becomes a saddler, and his saddles are so fine that Hereford's saddlers, losing every customer, conspire to kill the strangers; Pryderi's heir would fight, Manawydan counts the odds, and they move on. He becomes a shield-maker — the same beauty, the same conspiracy, the same dignified retreat. He becomes a shoemaker, gilding the shoes, and the cordwainers drive them out like the rest. Three trades, each mastered at first attempt, each surrendered rather than repaid in blood: the triads never forgot it, ranking Manawydan among the Three Golden Shoemakers of the Island of Britain. [Third Branch · Manawydan fab Llŷr] The Trial of the Mouse: Back in empty Dyfed, Manawydan sows three crofts of wheat, and they come up the finest in the land. The first croft, ripe for reaping, is found in the morning stripped to the bare straw; the second goes the same way. On the third night Manawydan keeps watch, and sees a host of mice descend on the ears, each mouse stripping an ear and carrying it off. He runs them down and catches one — the fattest, and slow, and heavy with young. He sets a miniature gallows on the gorsedd and condemns her as a thief. Then the ransomers come: a scholar, then a priest, then a bishop, each more richly robed than the last, each offering money for the felon's life, and to each Manawydan answers that he will not sell a convicted thief — until the bishop, pressed to name his terms, hears them whole: Pryderi and Rhiannon freed, the enchantment lifted from Dyfed, no vengeance taken on the mice, and no spell ever laid on the seven cantrefs again. The bishop is Llwyd fab Cil Coed, enchanter and friend of Gwawl fab Clud — Rhiannon's jilted suitor from the First Branch — and the whole desolation was his long revenge; the mice were his own household and warband under shape, and the fat one his wife. Pryderi comes back with the gate-hammers he had been made to carry, Rhiannon with the collars of asses about her neck, the mist lifts from Dyfed, and Manawydan keeps his word to the letter: not one mouse is harmed. It is the Mabinogi's most complete victory, and no sword is drawn in it.

Tell me a myth about "Bedwyr".

Input: Bedwyr

Bedwyr belongs to the oldest stratum of Arthurian tradition: the Welsh heroic material that predates Geoffrey of Monmouth and the whole romance edifice. His dossier is compact and precise — a poem's roster, a tale's three great episodes, two triads — and across all of it one fact never varies: where Cei goes, Bedwyr goes, and the one-handed man is never the lesser of the pair. [Pa gŵr? · Black Book of Carmarthen] The War-Band Remembered: The poem known from its opening line as Pa gŵr yv y porthaur? — 'What man is the gatekeeper?' — is the oldest Arthurian poem in Welsh: preserved in the thirteenth-century Black Book of Carmarthen, and itself composed perhaps centuries earlier. In it Arthur, halted at a fortress gate by the porter Glewlwyd Gafaelfawr, recites the roll of his companions to win entry, and Bedwyr stands in that roll beside Cei and Arthur's son Llacheu — already, in the earliest witness, one of the names Arthur speaks to prove his company. The poem is fragmentary — it breaks off mid-recitation — but its testimony matters beyond its length: it shows a Welsh Arthurian war-band whose heroes had their own deeds long before Geoffrey of Monmouth drew Arthur into Latin history, and Bedwyr is fixed in that founding generation. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The One-Handed Spearman: Culhwch ac Olwen, the earliest full Arthurian prose tale, gives Bedwyr his formal introduction when Arthur calls the companions for the quest of Olwen: Arthur called Bedwyr, 'who never shrank from any enterprise upon which Kai was bound. None was equal to him in swiftness throughout this Island except Arthur and Drych Ail Kibddar. And although he was one-handed, three warriors could not shed blood faster than he on the field of battle. Another property he had: his lance would produce a wound equal to those of nine opposing lances.' The great court-list earlier in the tale quietly extends the household: Amren son of Bedwyr stands among Arthur's huntsmen, and Eneuawc daughter of Bedwyr among the golden-chained maidens of the Island — the one-handed spearman with a son and daughter woven into the fabric of the court. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The Beard of Dillus the Bearded: No leash in the world could hold Drudwyn, the whelp of Greid son of Eri, save one made from the beard of Dillus Farfawc — and the beard was useless unless plucked from him alive with wooden tweezers, for once dead the bristles would turn brittle. As Cei and Bedwyr sat on a beacon cairn on the summit of Pumlumon, 'in the highest wind that ever was in the world', they spied smoke that did not bend with the wind, and found the greatest robber who ever fled from Arthur scorching a wild boar at his fire. They let him eat his fill and sleep; they shaped the wooden tweezers while he slept; Cei dug a pit beneath him, struck him into it, and together they plucked the beard clean and slew him. The leash was made and delivered to Arthur at Celli Wic — and Arthur answered with an englyn mocking Cei's deed, at which Cei's wrath was so great that the warriors of the Island could scarcely make peace between them, and Cei never again came to Arthur's aid. The episode that shows Bedwyr and Cei at their closest is the tale's own explanation of their company's end. [Culhwch ac Olwen] The Sword of Gwrnach and the Cauldron of Diwrnach: For the sword of Gwrnach the Giant, from whose castle no guest had ever returned alive, Cei went in alone under a false craft — the best burnisher of swords in the world — and won Bedwyr admission by a sign: the head of his lance would leave its shaft, draw blood from the wind, and settle on its shaft again. Inside, Cei polished the giant's sword, talked him out of his scabbard, and struck off his head with his own blade; the company despoiled the castle and bore the sword to Arthur's court by the beginning of the year. In Ireland, for the cauldron of Diwrnach Wyddel, the embassy's request was refused outright — and then Bedwyr arose and seized the cauldron and set it on the back of Hygwyd, Arthur's cauldron-bearer, while Llenlleawg Wyddel caught up Caledfwlch, and they slew Diwrnach and his company and fought their way back to the ship Prydwen, carrying the cauldron off full of Irish treasure. The two episodes are the pair's whole method: Cei's cunning at the gate, Bedwyr's hand on the prize. [Trioedd Ynys Prydein 21 · 26] The Diadem Above the Three: The Welsh triads keep the tradition's compressed memory, and they name Bedwyr twice — both times beside Cei. The triad of the Three Battle-Diademed of the Island of Britain names Drystan son of Tallwch, Hueil son of Caw, and Cei son of Cynyr — and then adds: and one was battle-diademed above all three of them, and that was Bedwyr son of Bedrawc. In the tradition's own arithmetic, the one-handed man outranks the three crowned warriors it had just named. The second naming is the triad's own joke at the war-band's expense. In the triad of the Three Powerful Swineherds, Drystan son of Tallwch kept the swine of March son of Meirchyawn while the swineherd carried a message to Essyllt — and Arthur and March and Cei and Bedwyr were there, all four, yet did not succeed in getting so much as one pigling, neither by force, nor by deception, nor by stealth. The greatest names in the Island, together, defeated by one watchful man and a herd of pigs. [Historia Regum Britanniae IX] Beduerus at Soissons: Geoffrey of Monmouth, drawing the Welsh heroes into his Latin history of the kings of Britain (c. 1136), makes Bedwyr into Beduerus: Arthur's cupbearer and constable of Normandy, one of the two companions — with Caius the seneschal — closest to the king. In the war against the Roman emperor Lucius, Beduerus falls in the fighting before Soissons — Geoffrey names his killer the giant Ritho of Mount Aravius, whom Arthur afterwards slew in single combat — and Arthur has him carried to Bayeux in Neustria, a city his own ancestors had built, and buried there with great lamentation. Geoffrey's account is pseudo-history, not Welsh tradition — but it fixed Bedwyr in the Latin chronicle line that Wace and Layamon would follow, and it is the hinge on which the Welsh Bedwyr turns into the Bedivere of European romance: the companion who dies in Arthur's service, far from home, mourned by the king he served.

Tell me a myth about "Hoori".

Input: Hoori

Hoori's mythology is the bridge between the heavenly descent of Ninigi and the earthly reign of Emperor Jimmu: a story of exchanged tools, a lost hook, a voyage to the dragon palace, a broken promise, and a line of kings. It is told in the Kojiki and repeated, with variations, in the Nihon Shoki. [Kojiki] The Exchanged Tools: The youngest son of Ninigi and Konohana-Sakuya-hime received from his father the bow , while his elder brother Hoderi received the fishhook — one son of the mountains, one of the sea, mirroring the division of the land itself (Kojiki I). Hoori proposed that they exchange tools for a single day: he would try his brother's fortune with the hook, Hoderi the mountains with the bow. The day went well for no one. Hoori, inexpert at the shore, lost the borrowed hook in the sea, and when he dived and dragged the bottom it could not be found. Hoderi refused every substitute — first his own sword, then five hundred mother-of-pearl hooks, then a thousand — demanding back the one original hook, the single object through which a man's fortune was thought to run. The impossible demand drives the younger brother out of the human world and down into the sea: the quarrel over one small thing is what opens the door to the gods. [Kojiki] The Dragon Palace of Watasumi: Following the counsel of an old man on the beach — one of the passing kami who advise heroes at their lowest hour — Hoori sat on the bough of a tree that bent over the waves until the tide carried him down through a gateway into the undersea palace of Watasumi-no-kami , the sea deity. There he was welcomed, bathed, feasted, and married to the sea god's daughter Toyotama-hime , the 'Abundant-Jewel Princess' (Kojiki I). When Hoori confessed why he had come, Toyotama's brother searched the sea and recovered the lost hook from the throat of a red sea-bream. Watasumi then gave his son-in-law two treasures — the tide-flowing jewel and the tide-ebbing jewel, with which any sea can be raised or stilled — and taught him the ruse by which a proud man is broken: do not answer rage with rage, but mock it gently as it rages , and its strength will spend itself against your calm. The palace gives the exiled brother everything his own shore withheld: a wife, the hook, and a strategy. [Kojiki] The Mocked Brother and the Covenant: Hoori returned to land and waited on the beach. When Hoderi came raging across the strand, Hoori sang a mocking song — as the Kojiki has it, like the bushes on the shore his brother's beard was tangled, like the drifting seaweed his rage floated aimlessly — and Hoderi attacked. Hoori raised the tide-flowing jewel, and the sea rose to Hoderi's neck; Hoderi begged and wept, and Hoori raised the ebbing jewel and spared him (Kojiki I). The brothers made peace on a new order: Hoderi would keep the watery ways, and his descendants would serve Hoori's line forever. Thus the sea-fortune and the mountain-fortune were divided as they still are in Japan — and the humbler brother, who had lost everything in the water, came home owning both the land and the sea's obedience. The myth's arithmetic is deliberate: the borrowed hook cost nothing to replace, but the brotherly covenant it purchased was the real prize. [Kojiki] The Broken Taboo and the First Emperor: Toyotama came up from the sea to bear her child, but first she built a parturition hut roofed with cormorant feathers and laid down the law that Hoori must not look inside. Curiosity — the flaw and the engine of this whole cycle — overcame him. He peeked and saw his wife in her true shape, a great sea-dragon coiled in the hut; mortified, Toyotama abandoned the land and the newborn, sending her sister Tamayori-hime in her place with a parting song. The child, Ugayafukiaezu , was raised by his aunt, married her in time, and their son was Kamuyamato-Iwarebiko — better known as Emperor Jimmu , first emperor of Japan (Kojiki I; Nihon Shoki I). Hoori's one act of disobedience costs him his wife, yet it leaves the imperial line on land, guarded by sea and mountain at once. The sources read the episode without apology: the line of emperors begins exactly where the promise was broken.

[Avataṃsaka Sūtra] The Buddha Whose Body Is the Cosmos: The Avataṃsaka Sūtra — the Flower Garland, first translated into Chinese by Buddhabhadra in 420 CE — opens on a scale no other scripture attempts: Vairocana enthroned not in a grove but in the dharmadhātu itself, the Dharma-realm, every pore of his body a world-system, every atom of every world containing all the others, the whole interpenetrating without confusion like the chambers of Indra's net, where a jewel at every crossing mirrors every other jewel, and each mirrored jewel mirrors the rest to infinity. The sūtra's visions are not allegories but descriptions: the cosmos is the Buddha's body, and the Buddha's body is the cosmos explaining itself. The Huayan masters drew the conclusion that became Chinese Buddhism's deepest contribution — li shih wu ai , the unobstructed interpenetration of principle and phenomena. It is the largest picture of interdependence ever painted: nothing exists alone, and the Great Sun is the name for the whole net seen at once. [Mahāvairocana Sūtra] The Sun That Preaches Without Words: The esoteric tradition's own charters, the Mahāvairocana Sūtra and its twin the Tattvasaṃgraha — translated into Chinese in 724–725 by the Indian master Śubhakarasiṃha with the commentary of the Chinese astronomer-monk Yixing — present the cosmic Buddha not as a person among persons but as the dharmakāya, the Dharma-body, whose sermon is reality's ongoing act of existing. The sūtra's root metaphor is the sun: as the sun illuminates all things without discriminating among them, the Buddha's wisdom shines on all beings without choosing favorites — and the moon's light, borrowed and returned, stands for the teaching as beings receive it. Kūkai gave the idea its boldest Japanese formula: hosshin seppō , the dharmakāya itself preaches. Mountains, rivers, the sound of rain — for Shingon these are not metaphors for the teaching but the teaching in progress, and the maṇḍala is the lesson read as a map. The myth dissolves the distance between scripture and weather. [Shingon] Kūkai and the Two Maṇḍalas: In 804 the monk Kūkai sailed to Tang China; at Qinglong monastery in Chang'an the patriarch Huiguo, recognizing him on sight as his destined successor, transmitted to him the Womb and Diamond maṇḍalas — the two great maps of Mahāvairocana's body and wisdom — in the space of a few months, and in 806 Kūkai carried them home. In 816 he vowed a mountain monastery on Kōya-san, high in the cedar forests of Kii, consecrated 819; in 823 the court granted him Tō-ji in Kyoto as the esoteric school's capital seat; and there he built a school in which ritual, art, calligraphy, and philosophy are one act — to move through the maṇḍala in ceremony is to remember that one is made of the same light as its center. The tradition holds that Kūkai never died: he sits in eternal meditation in his tomb on Kōya-san, awaiting Maitreya. Shingon remains one of the largest living Vajrayāna communities outside Tibet — two maṇḍalas, still teaching. [Nara] The Emperor's Great Buddha: In 743, with rebellion in the east and smallpox scything the cities, Emperor Shōmu issued his proclamation (recorded in the Shoku Nihongi ) commanding a great bronze Vairocana — the Nara rendering of the cosmic Buddha, read in the Fujiwara-kyō and Nara court as the Avataṃsaka 's central figure — so that the realm itself might be sheltered within the Buddha's body. The casting bankrupted and unified the provinces: the court taxed the road-corvée and conscripted the metal of the whole archipelago, and abbots wrote that heaven answered with good harvests. The Tōdai-ji Daibutsu, some fifteen meters of gilt bronze, was consecrated in 752 before ten thousand monks, the Indian monk Bodhisena daishing the eyes — kaigen , the ceremony of opening the eyes, held exactly as texts prescribed. It was the largest bronze casting of its age, bankrolled by a court that believed the Avataṃsaka's cosmos could shelter a state. The statue still sits in its hall, the Great Sun in metal. [Huayan] Fazang's Golden Lion: The greatest teacher the Avataṃsaka ever found was a Sogdian-born prodigy in the Tang capital. Fazang, third patriarch of the Huayan school, was called to lecture on the sūtra before Empress Wu Zetian — and, the tradition recorded in his own Jin shizi zhang (Treatise on the Golden Lion), he chose his teaching-prop with imperial wit: a gilded lion from the palace itself. The lion's gold, he explained, is the principle, li; its form — eyes, ears, limbs, roar — is the phenomena, shi. Melt the gold and no lion remains, yet never for an instant was there gold that was not the lion: neither precedes the other, each pervades the other, and every hair of the mane contains the whole beast. The empress was enlightened on the spot, by court chronicle's account, and Huayan became the Tang's state philosophy of totality. The parable endures because it makes interdependence something you can hold: a lion of gold, a cosmos of light.

Tell me a myth about "Vasubandhu".

Input: Vasubandhu

Vasubandhu was a historical philosopher, not a mythological figure — a monk of Puruṣapura (Peshawar) who, the early Tibetan biographies say, wrote the Abhidharmakośa as a Sarvāstivādin critic and then embraced the Yogācāra Mahāyāna of his half-brother Asaṅga. His 'myths' are the legends his tradition grew around a real life. [The Kośa] Three Years in Seclusion: The Tibetan biographies recount that Vasubandhu withdrew into seclusion to master the Abhidharma of the Kashmir Sarvāstivādins, and emerged with the Abhidharmakośa — six hundred verses (kārikā) of flawless eight-syllable metre that summarized the entire system. When the Kashmir masters admired the verses but missed their own subtlety, he added an auto-commentary (bhāṣya) of his own in which, tradition says, he quietly refuted them. The Kośa became what it remains: the one Abhidharma text every later school — Theravāda, Mahāyāna, and the Tibetan lineages — had to study, debate, or answer, translated in its entirety into Chinese by Xuanzang and memorized in fragments by generations of monks from Kashmir to Kyoto. Its author's own allegiance was already drifting as he wrote: the commentary, tradition says, shows the Sautrāntika reservations that would later make his conversion credible. To condense a library into verse, and the verse into a single lifetime, is the legend's whole point: scholarship can be a kind of asceticism. [Conversion] The Begging Letter of Asaṅga: Vasubandhu had mocked the Mahāyāna as a corruption of the Buddha's teaching, calling its scriptures fabrications. His elder half-brother Asaṅga, already a great Yogācāra teacher, sent him no rebuttal — only a note reporting that he was dying, and begging Vasubandhu to recite the Mahāyāna sūtras for him. Struck by the affection of the request, Vasubandhu read them, found them profound, and entered the Mahāyāna himself. The story is hagiography — no Indian source records it independently — yet it encodes the tradition's own account of its greatest conversion: Vasubandhu did not abandon analysis for devotion. He turned the same razor-sharp mind to the 'mind-only' philosophy, composing the Twenty Verses (Viṁśikā) and the Thirty Verses (Triṁśikā) that define the Yogācāra, and the two halves of his career became one continuous argument about how carefully the world must be taken apart before it can be seen whole. [The Debate] The Victory over Vasurāta: The biographies carry Vasubandhu to the courts of northern India, where the grammarian-philosopher Vasurāta, champion of an opposing school, had humiliated all comers. Vasubandhu entered the contest — the tradition describes a great assembly of rival teachers and lay patrons gathered to watch — and his opponent was worsted. After the debate he was offered a great patron's gold — and the legends insist that, as a monk, he spent the wealth on works of benefit to the saṅgha and on gifts to the poor. The story matters less as history than as the template it sets: the philosopher's victory is measured not in refutation but in what the victor refuses to keep. Every medieval debate culture of the Buddhist world — Nālandā's, Tibet's, Japan's — repeated this scene with Vasubandhu's name in it, and his reputation as the undefeated champion of two successive orthodoxies made the later conversion legend necessary: only love, the tradition decided, could have beaten him. [The Problem] One Vasubandhu or Two?: Modern scholarship has had to ask whether one man could have written both the Kośa's analytical Abhidharma and the Yogācāra's visionary metaphysics. Erich Frauwallner (1951) argued the dates fit a single long life; others have proposed two Vasubandhus — the Yogācāra co-founder and a later Kośa author — and the question is still argued in the journals. The tradition itself never doubted: one Vasubandhu, brother of Asaṅga, whose conversion joined the two oeuvres into a single career — and the hagiographies even extend that life into legend, saying he ended it in the Pure Land of Amitābha, or in Nepal, depending on which strand one follows. The modern debate is itself a tribute: few ancient authors are so prolific and so consistent in brilliance that posterity must ask whether they were two people.

Tell me a myth about "Arhat".

Input: Arhat

The arhat has no biography because the arhat is a hundred biographies — the finished saints of the Theragāthā and Therīgāthā, the chief disciples of the canon, and in China a band of sixteen immortals commanded to wait out the ages for the next Buddha. [The Word] Worthy of Gifts: Arhat comes from √ arh , "to deserve, to be worthy," with the participle -at — "the worthy one," one deserving of the alms of gods and men. The Buddha claimed it as his own foremost title: in the canonical litany he is arahaṃ sammāsambuddho , "arahant, fully self-awakened" — a claim whose audacity the Udāna records being tested in his lifetime, when rivals demanded he prove it. The commentarial definition sharpens the word into a checklist: one who has destroyed the taints ( āsava ), lived the holy life, done what had to be done, laid down the burden, and knows "there is no more of this." The Jaina tradition uses the same word in parallel: its twenty-four tīrthaṅkaras are arhats , worthy ones who ford the flood of rebirth. The mythic weight of a title: Buddhism made holiness a completed task, not a birth — and gave it a word anyone could check. [The Chiefs] Sāriputta and Moggallāna: The Buddha named his two greatest arahants in the Etadagga verses (AN 1): Sāriputta , foremost in great wisdom — the Dhamma's marshal, who could unfold a single line into a hundred meanings and who, questioned on his deathbed in the Sāriputta Sutta (SN 47.19), replied only that there was nowhere he had ever clung; and Moggallāna , foremost in psychic powers, who humbled Brahmā's pride by shaking the Vejayanta palace with a toe (DN 11, Kevaṭṭa Sutta ). Both were murdered — Moggallāna beaten to death by brigands — the Buddha predicting that the pair would die as the twin sāla trees fall. The Theragāthā lets the arahants speak in their own voices: "Cut down the whole forest of craving, not just one tree; from the jungle of craving, fear is born." The ideal is given a human face twice — the thinker and the wonder-worker — and both faces end in the one death arahants cannot refuse. [The Path] Four Gates to the Deathless: Arahantship is the fourth and last gate. The canon maps the road precisely: the stream-enterer (sotāpanna), certain of awakening, never again reborn lower than human; the once-returner (sakadāgāmin), who comes back once to this world; the non-returner (anāgāmin), who awakens in a higher heaven and does not return at all; and the arahant , freed here and now. The decisive faculty is stated everywhere and nowhere better than the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta (MN 10): mindfulness of body, feelings, mind, and dhammas — "the direct path for the purification of beings, for the overcoming of sorrow." Fifteen centuries later Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga (5th c. CE) welded the whole road into one manual, still the map of Theravāda practice. The interpretive core: holiness is gradual, inspectable, and irreversible — a ladder whose rungs can be named, and whose top rung is the end of needing anything, forever. [The Sixteen] The Lohans Who Guard the Dharma: Chinese Buddhism gave the arahants a second life as luohan — sixteen great disciples the Buddha, before his parinirvāṇa, commanded to remain in the world without entering final nirvāṇa until Maitreya comes. Their charter text, Xuanzang's 654 translation of Nandimitra's Record of the Duration of the Dharma , names them — Mahākāśyapa, Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya, Kanakavatsa, Subhūti, Nandimitra himself and the rest — each assigned a mountain, a retinue, and a district of the earth to protect. The painter Guanxiu (10th c.) gave them their immortal faces, gaunt and strange, and his line was copied for a thousand years; Ming temples house ranks of gilded lohans, five hundred strong, each with his own demon, dragon, or tiger. The myth is a quiet reversal: the extinct ideal of early Buddhism — the saint who is done — is drafted as a permanent garrison, waiting out the ages at their posts for the next Buddha, deathless on duty.

Tell me a myth about "Śākyamuni".

Input: Śākyamuni

The life of Śākyamuni is the best-attested sacred biography of the ancient world — told in the Pāli Nikāyas, versified by Aśvaghoṣa, expanded in the Nidānakathā and the Lalitavistara, and anchored in the ground by Aśoka's own inscriptions. [Nidānakathā / Lalitavistara] The Birth at Lumbinī: Queen Māyā, traveling to her father's house, gave birth standing in the grove at Lumbinī, holding the branch of a sāla tree; the child took seven steps and declared this his last birth. The legends multiplied — the shower of blossoms, the two streams of water, the prophecy of the sage Asita — but the place is fixed in stone: Aśoka's pillar at Rummindei, raised in his twentieth regnal year, reads in plain Prakrit, hida budhe jāte sakyamuni — "here the Buddha Śākyamuni was born." It is the only birthplace of a world teacher certified by a contemporary emperor. [Ariyapariyesanā Sutta] The Four Sights and the Going Forth: Sheltered in three palaces, the young Śākyan saw what his father had fenced out: an old man, a sick man, a corpse, and a wandering ascetic — the four sights the later tradition makes the hinge of his life. In the Majjhima Nikāya's Ariyapariyesanā Sutta (MN 26) he tells it himself: he shaved his hair, put on the ochre robe, and went forth from home into homelessness while still young, in the prime of life, with his parents weeping. The great renunciation — the night ride on Kaṇṭhaka with the groom Channa — became Buddhist art's first epic scene. [SN 56.11] The Awakening and the First Turning: Six years of austerities on the Nairañjanā brought him to the edge of death and the discovery of the middle way; seated under the Bodhi tree at Uruvelā he withstood Māra's assault, touched the earth as his witness, and by dawn saw the four noble truths and the chain of dependent arising. Weeks later, in the deer park at Ṛṣipatana near Benares — Sarnath — he taught the five ascetics the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (SN 56.11), the setting-in-motion of the wheel: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the eightfold path. The sermon is preserved in every Buddhist canon; the wheel he turned has not stopped. [Mahāparinibbāna Sutta] The Last Days at Kusinārā: The Dīgha Nikāya's Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16) follows his last journey with a chronicler's eye: the meal offered by the smith Cunda, the sickness, the couch laid northward between twin sāla trees in the Mallas' grove at Kusinārā, which burst into blossom out of season. His last instruction was a refusal of permanence itself: "All conditioned things are of a nature to decay — strive on with diligence." The Mallas cremated him as a universal monarch, and his relics were divided into eight shares and enshrined in stupas — the beginning of Buddhist sacred architecture.
