Tell me a myth about "Diāna".

Input: Diāna

Roman myth largely retells Artemis' stories under Diāna's name — but her cult institutions are Italy's own, older than the stories, and stranger: a grove ruled by an armed fugitive, a federal temple built as an act of constitutional politics, and a goddess whose most famous myth is a warning about looking. [The Bath] Actaeon: It is Ovid who gives the Roman telling its shape ( Metamorphoses 3.138–252), and he gives it a moral that is pure Diāna: it is about seeing, not lust. Actaeon, out hunting at noon with his hounds and his horses, wanders off — whether by fate or by error, the poet hedges — into a valley where a natural arch of rock drips with spring water, and there the goddess is bathing, her nymphs crowding to shield her. Too late: he has seen. She catches up a handful of the spring and sprinkles him — 'now you may tell that you saw me, if you can' — and the antlers begin, the neck lengthens, the hands become feet, and the hunter becomes the stag. Worse follows: his own pack, which knows only the shape of prey, does not know its master's voice, and the hounds tear him down while he cries his own name. The myth is the goddess's charter: the wild is not a picture. To look at it as an object is already to have entered the hunt — on the wrong side. [The Grove] The King of the Wood: Strabo, a Greek geographer who knew Italy well, records the strangest priesthood in the Roman world (5.3.12): beside a lake in the Alban hills sacred to Diāna — Lake Nemi, which the Romans called Diana's Mirror — there stood a tree from which it was forbidden to break a bough, and the sanctuary's priest was always a runaway slave, armed with a sword, who had won his office by plucking the bough and killing his predecessor in single combat, and who held it thereafter against the next challenger, sword drawn. Ovid addresses the custom in the Fasti (3.263–272): when the priest who slew the slayer keeps watch in the lonely grove. The rite was already archaic in the Augustan age; two thousand years later it opened Frazer's Golden Bough , the book that made comparative religion a public science. The grove encodes a hard theology of the wild: possession of the sacred is never secure — it must be defended by the same violence by which it was taken, forever, at the edge of a lake that only reflects. [The Refuge] Hippolytus Reborn: Roman tradition gave Nemi a founding ghost. Virgil tells it in half a dozen lines ( Aeneid 7.761–782): Virbius, the most beautiful of men, son of Hippolytus and Aricia, was raised in the goddess's grove, where horses are banned — for Hippolytus was the Greek hunter dragged to death by his own horses, and the chaste son of Theseus could not be trusted near them. Ovid gives the whole story ( Metamorphoses 15.497–546): Hippolytus, dragged to pieces and brought back from the dead by Aesculapius's art at Diāna's pleading, was hidden by the goddess in her Italian grove and given a new name — Virbius, vir bis , 'twice a man.' The myth is the Roman answer to the Greek tragedy: where the Greek story kills the hunter who rejected love, the Italian sanctuary shelters and rebirths him. Nemi's grove is a hospital for the twice-living — the place where even the tragic refuse of Greek myth is given a second body and a new name, under Roman protection. [The Alliance] The Aventine Charter: Her greatest temple was a constitution. Dionysius of Halicarnassus ( Antiquitates Romanae 4.25–26) describes the temple of Diāna that Servius Tullius built on the Aventine as the common sanctuary of the Latin peoples — a federal shrine where the cities of Latium met the Romans as equals, deliberately built in the Greek manner. Livy (1.45.2) fixes the foundation in Servius' reign. The dedication produced one of those characteristic Roman origin-stories about priority: at the joint festival, a Sabine declared his own ox the finest animal present and its entrails his by right; the cunning Roman priest sacrificed the beast first and carried off the liver, and the arbitration of the dispute confirmed that precedence belongs to whoever acts, not whoever talks. The sanctuary doubled as an asylum, sheltering fugitive slaves and debtors — fittingly, since its priest at Nemi was himself a fugitive. Diāna's Aventine was the one altar in Italy where Rome's future subjects practiced being partners, and the goddess of the wild presided over the city's oldest experiment in federalism. [The Maiden] Camilla, the Volscian: Virgil's last Italian heroine belongs to Diāna. Metabus, king of the Volscians and hated by his own people, fled with his infant daughter when his city burned; blockaded at the flooded river Amasenus, he lashed the baby to his spear, called on the goddess of the woods, and hurled her across the torrent — and she was caught, or the river-goddess caught her. Swearing her to virginity and to the hunt, he raised her in the wilderness, and she became the warrior-maiden of the Italian war in the Aeneid : fleet of foot, racing the wind itself, her spear-work compared to an Amazon's (7.803–817). She falls to the hidden spear of Arruns, and Diāna answers: her nymph Opis, posted on a hill for exactly this, plants an arrow in Arruns and speaks the poem's bitterest epitaph — her spoils will never be enjoyed (11.532–724). Camilla is the goddess's price and her boast: the wild breeds loyalty, and even the losing side of history gets a divine witness.

Tell me a myth about "Neptūnus".

Input: Neptūnus

Rome gave Neptūnus few native myths — his biography is Poseidṓn's translated — but the festival and the horse-cult are Italy's own, older than the sea-borrowing. [The Drought] The Huts of Branches: The Neptunalia of July 23 is Rome's oldest water rite, and Festus' dictionary preserves its strangest detail: the people kept holiday in huts woven of leafy branches — umbrae , 'shades' — drinking and feasting in the green dark of their own making while the sun stood at the year's hottest (Festus, s.v. Neptunalia). The antiquarians argued about the god's name — Varro (De lingua Latina 5.72) weighs a derivation from nubere , 'to cover,' as the sky covers the earth — but the festival's meaning needs no philology: it is a prayer said in the vocabulary of architecture, shade and water asked of the power who withholds them. Neptūnus' first realm was the spring, the stream, the well that keeps a farm alive; the Mediterranean, with its fleets and fortunes, was the empire's later gift to him. Every arbour was a small theology: that water, like mercy, is most worth begging for when it is scarcest. [The Horse] Lord of the Race: As Neptūnus Equester he shared the underground altar of Consus, the old god of the stored grain whose altar lay buried near the Circus Maximus and was uncovered only for his games (Tertullian, De spectaculis 5). At the Consualia in August, horses and mules were garlanded and rested from their labor, and chariots raced for the year's honor. It was at one such festival that Romulus staged the seizure of the Sabine women, inviting the neighboring tribes to watch the games and then giving the signal (Livy 1.9; Plutarch, Romulus 14). Rome's foundation story thus begins at Neptūnus' racetrack, with the horses watching: the god of the hidden granary and the god of the hidden water meet underground, and above them the city performs its oldest transaction — spectacle in exchange for wives, horses in exchange for luck. The partnership makes economic sense the farmers understood: the horse pulls the plough to the water, and both, properly honored, pull the city through the year. [The Contest] Minerva and the City: Roman retellings kept the Greek contest for Athens and read it as a civic lesson. Poseidōn struck the rock of the Acropolis with his trident and brought forth either the salt spring — Herodotus (8.55) saw the marks of the trident still — or, in another version, the first horse (Apollodorus 3.14.1). Athēnâ's olive won the city's name, and the god of force went away sullen, his spring turning salty in his anger. Roman authors delighted in the moral: wisdom outranks strength, and the tree that feeds beats the wave that drowns — a reading that let the conquerors of the Mediterranean patronize the sea they had just conquered. But the story keeps a second edge that Rome could not blunt: the loser never leaves. The salt spring stayed on the Acropolis, and Neptūnus stayed in the Roman calendar, and the contest is never really finished — every harbor is an olive and a trident still arguing about which of them feeds the city. [The Plea] Agrippa at Naulochus: Roman sea-power came late, and when it came it dedicated itself. In 36 BCE Marcus Agrippa destroyed the fleet of Sextus Pompeius at Naulochus, the decisive victory of the war against the pirate-prince, and the honor was assigned to Neptūnus: Appian (Bellum Civile 5.118) records that Agrippa was awarded a golden crown adorned with ships' prows — the corona rostrata , minted afterward on coins. Vergil, closing the shield of Aeneas, had already pictured the sea-god ranged among Octavian's gods at Actium (Aeneid 8.698). The gesture is the interpretatio Romana in action: a borrowed god made genuinely Roman by a Roman victory, his temple and games the empire's thank-you note to the water that had nearly been lost. By the high empire, altars to Neptūnus stood from Ostia to the Tyne — sailors' religion, contracted port by port, where every crossing is a small Naulochus and every harbor a god's fee.

Tell me a myth about "Aṃśa".

Input: Aṃśa

Aṃśa has no single great narrative — like many Vedic gods, he is a function given face: the apportionment that the sacrifice performs and the year repeats. His mythology is the theology of the share, told by the hymns that divide, the Brāhmaṇas that legislate the division, and the Purāṇas that calendar it. [The Twelve] Son of Aditi: The Ṛgveda knows the Ādityas as the sons of Aditi — 'the unbound' — the solar powers who guard ṛta , cosmic order, and punish the oath-breaker; hymns such as 2.27 invoke them as the strong sons of the boundless mother, each one a face of the one sun's law. The later tradition counts them as twelve, one for each month of the year, and the roster survives in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (6.6.38–39): Dhātā, Mitra, Aryamā, Śakra, Varuṇa, Aṃśa , Bhaga, Vivasvān, Pūṣā, Savitā, Tvaṣṭā, Viṣṇu. Aṃśa stands in the list exactly where his name says he must: among the guardians of the covenant, the enforcers of what is due. A god whose name is the word for 'share' is a theology you can parse at sight — he is the portion, personified, and his inclusion among the law-keeping suns declares that fair division is not bookkeeping but cosmic order. [The Sacrifice] Every God a Share: The Vedic sacrifice is an economy of portions. The hymn distributes the offering — 'this share to Agni, this to Soma' — and the Brāhmaṇas legislate that the gods' shares were fixed at the beginning of things: the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1.7.3–4) tells how the gods and the anti-gods contended for the sacrifice, how the gods took it for their own and assigned its parts — the ghee, the grains, the portions of the carcass — so that every deity receives the measure that is his. Aṃśa is the personification of that fixing: without the allotted share, no ritual holds, no inheritance stands, no year completes. The deepest grammar of the idea is already in the Puruṣa Sūkta (Ṛgveda 10.90.11–14), where the gods divide the primal being himself — from whose mouth, arms, thighs, and feet the orders of society arise. Creation, in this vision, is a division; and the share-god is creation's own arithmetic made divine. [The Contest] The Dispute over the Portion: The Brāhmaṇas are honest that the gods did not win their shares by innocence alone. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa's telling (1.7.3–4), the gods and the asuras — both children of Prajāpati — strove for the worlds and the sacrifice; the gods prevailed by wit and stratagem, and the asuras were driven down. The myth's lesson is the god's nature: a share is never neutral — it is the shape of justice or of theft, and Aṃśa's name sits on the scale. The same Brāhmaṇic imagination keeps the warning concrete in stories of stolen soma and rigged dice: what is portioned out can be portioned wrongly, and the cosmos notices. This is why the hymns place the share-god among the Ādityas, the guardians of ṛta, rather than among the givers of boons. The share is not a gift but a right; its measure is the oldest form of justice there is — and its theft the oldest crime. [The Year] The Twelve Suns: Purāṇic astronomy assigns each month to one of the twelve Ādityas — the dvādaśāditya of Bhāgavata Purāṇa 12.11.27–32, where the sun of each month presides over a season's work from his own station, and the year is the sum of their turns. The Veda had already imaged it: the famous wheel of Ṛgveda 1.164.11, 'set with twelve spokes', upon which seven hundred twenty children of Agni stand — the days and nights riding the year's rim. For Aṃśa the correspondence is exact: the year is the oldest inheritance, and each month its share. His name outlived his cult in the same discipline — Jyotiṣa divides every sign of the zodiac into nine navāṃśa , 'ninth-shares', the harmonic chart without which no horoscope is read. His cult needed no image and no temple: only the accurate turning of the solar year, worshipped every morning in the Gāyatrī that all twelve suns share.

Tell me a myth about "Pūṣan".

Input: Pūṣan

Pūṣan is the most companionable of Vedic gods: where others blaze, he accompanies. His myths are all journeys — of cattle, of brides, of the dead — and one memorable injury. [The Escort] Guide of Souls: The Ṛgveda’s funeral hymn entrusts the dead to him with startling tenderness: ‘May Pūṣan take your hand and lead you onward; may the two Aśvins, mounted on their chariot, carry you; go to the well-prepared place, go where the fathers have gone before’ (RV 10.17). He is chosen because he knows every road: the hymns repeat that he travels the paths between heaven and earth daily at the sun’s flank, and that no path of his is ever blocked. Where Yama rules the dead and Agni carries the offering, Pūṣan is the escort — the god whose whole office is accompaniment. The Vedic poets seem to have understood something modern grief still discovers: what the dying most need is not a judge but a guide who knows the way by heart, having walked it every day of the world’s turning. The herdsman who loses no animal from the herd is exactly the god to trust with a soul. [The Wedding] The Giving of Sūryā: At the wedding of the Sun-maiden Sūryā — the Ṛgveda’s great marriage hymn, RV 10.85 — the gods themselves form the procession: Mitra, Varuna, and Aryaman escort her, the Aśvins are her eager suitors, and Soma wins her, ‘for Soma her father gave the maiden’. Pūṣan has the office that outlasts them all: as her kinsman he takes the bride’s hand to give her away — the kanyādāna performed by a god. The hymn’s formulas did not stay in the book. They passed into the living Hindu wedding, where verses of the Sūryā-sūkta are still recited as the father places his daughter’s hand in the groom’s — which means that at millions of weddings every year, Pūṣan is still, liturgically, the one conducting the bride down the aisle. The Veda here is not an artifact but a living officiant: the guide of the road presides over the shortest and most auspicious journey a person makes. [The Teeth] The Gruel of Dakṣa’s Rite: When Rudra, excluded from Dakṣa’s great sacrifice, fell upon it in wrath, the gods scattered — and Pūṣan, caught at the moment of ruin with the offering in his mouth, took the blow meant for the rite: his teeth were smashed out (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.7.3–4). The Brāhmaṇas preserve the wound in the liturgy itself: Pūṣan alone among the gods receives karambha , a gruel of ground grain, precisely because he cannot chew. It is the Vedic taste for exact, even comic piety — the god’s injury written into his menu — but the theology beneath the joke is precise: ritual violence leaves permanent marks on the divine body, and the tradition does not hide them; it accommodates them, forever. The gruel-offering is the Veda’s gentlest doctrine. The toothless mouth did not end Pūṣan’s service; it only changed what the service could receive — and the liturgy, feeding him accordingly, taught the community its own lesson in caring for the scarred. [The Finding] Seeker of Lost Cattle: The hymns beg him for the oldest pastoral miracle: ‘Pūṣan, bring back what has strayed; Pūṣan, show us the road’ (RV 6.53–54). He is invoked over lost cattle, lost travelers, lost paths — the god who finds what the world mislays, because he follows the sun and nothing hidden escapes that light. Even his own equipment once failed him: his chariot-wheel broke on the road, and it was the Aśvins, the divine physicians, who fashioned him a new one (RV 1.119) — the guide of the whole pantheon briefly stranded, and rescued by the gods of healing. The episode is a small masterpiece of Vedic realism: the one who accompanies everyone needs accompaniment too, and receives it. That reciprocity is the deepest note in his cult. Pūṣan does not blaze like Sūrya or thunder like Indra; he keeps the herd moving, finds the strayed, and accepts — with the gruel, with the mended wheel — the community’s duty of care for its own guide.

Tell me a myth about "Pángǔ".

Input: Pángǔ

Pángǔ's myth exists in two sentences of immense consequence, recorded by Xú Zhěng in the 3rd century CE — and expanded by a civilization into its canonical account of how the world began. [The Egg] Three-Five Calendar Record: Xú Zhěng's Sānwǔ lìjì (3rd century CE, preserved in later encyclopedias) gives the founding text: 'Heaven and earth were chaos like a hen's egg, and Pángǔ was born within it. After eighteen thousand years, heaven and earth opened: the bright, light qì rose to become heaven; the dark, heavy qì sank to become earth. Pángǔ stood between them, changing nine times daily — heaven rising ten feet a day, earth thickening ten feet, and Pángǔ growing ten feet — for eighteen thousand years more, until heaven stood ninety thousand li above the earth.' The arithmetic is the myth's own poetry: the world is not spoken into being but pushed apart by increments, against a measurable resistance — creation as the first and longest labor, and the giant as the one who never stops growing because his work is never done. [The Death] The Body Becomes the World: When the separation was fixed, Pángǔ died — and the transformation began, in the same text's most famous lines: his breath became wind and cloud, his voice thunder, his left eye the sun and his right the moon, his four limbs the four sacred mountains, his blood the rivers, his veins the roads, his flesh the soil, his hair the stars, his skin and body-hair grass and trees, his sweat the rain — and, in the most anthropologically piquant line, the fleas and lice of his body, quickened by the wind, became the black-haired people. Nothing in the list is wasted and nothing is decorative: the myth insists that geography is biography — that every mountain is a limb and every river a vein — so that to wound the landscape is to wound the body one lives inside. It is the world's most complete statement of the sacredness of place. [The Late Arrival] China's Youngest Creator: The myth's strangest fact is its date: no pre-Han text mentions Pángǔ, and the Sānwǔ lìjì itself has to be reconstructed from quotations in medieval encyclopedias, for the original is lost. Scholars trace his entry through southern traditions — the Yao and Miao genealogies of the dog-ancestor Pán Hù, phonetically adjacent, from the very region the later sources call Pángǔ country — absorbed and cosmicized in the Wei-Jin centuries, when the north's older creation-by-culture-hero had left a vacancy at the very beginning. China's canonical creation is thus a relative newcomer, adopted so completely that every schoolchild now learns it as the oldest story — a case of a myth winning by arriving last, exactly when the civilization needed a single name to put at the head of time. [The Variants] Folk Versions and a Southern Country: By the sixth century the giant had accumulated regional tellings, and Rèn Fáng's Shùyì jì ('Records of Strange Matters', c. 500 CE) preserves the collated harvest. The folk versions map his body onto the sacred mountains with cheerful disagreement: in one, his head became the Eastern Marchmount, his belly the Central, his limbs the Southern and Northern, his feet the Western; in another, his tears became the rivers, his breath the wind, his voice thunder, his pupils lightning — and his moods the weather, his gladness clearing the sky and his anger clouding it (Shùyì jì, quoting what it calls Qín-Hàn popular sayings). The most remarkable entry records that in the southern sea there was a Pángǔ country whose people bore Pángǔ as their surname — a whole people claiming descent from the giant. And in the Wú-Chǔ region south of the Yangtze, the tellers made him a married pair: Pángǔ and his wife, 'the beginning of yin and yang.' The creator was still growing new versions four centuries after his first written breath — evidence that China never finished deciding what its youngest god meant.

Tell me a myth about "Honshū".

Input: Honshū

Honshū's mythology is the national charter itself: the Kojiki's island-birth, the sun goddess's gift of the land, and the descent of her grandson to rule it. [The Birth] The Islands from the Spear: The Kojiki opens on the heavenly bridge: Izanagi and Izanami stir the ocean with the jewelled spear, and from the brine dripping from its point the first island coagulates. Descending, they wed and give birth to the islands of Japan — the "great eight islands" culminating in Ōyashima — and then to the kami of wind, sea, mountain, and tree. The archipelago is not created but born: the land is kin. [The Sun] Amaterasu's Realm: When the sun goddess Amaterasu withdrew into the Heavenly Rock-Cave — outraged by her brother Susanoo's rampage — the world went dark until the gods' comic dance lured her out. Her mirror, hung outside the cave, caught her own light back to her; that mirror rests at Ise on Honshū's Kii coast, and her shrine there has been ritually rebuilt every twenty years for thirteen centuries: the island's heartwood, renewed. [The Descent] Ninigi and the Rice Land: Amaterasu sent her grandson Ninigi down from heaven to rule the "Land of Fair Rice-ears of the Fertile Reed-plain" — the Kojiki's name for Honshū's heartland — bearing the three regalia. His great-grandson Jimmu conquered eastward to Yamato and became the first emperor: the mythic bridge from island-birth to imperial genealogy, anchored to real ground in Nara's basin. [The Yielding] Ōkuninushi Surrenders the Land: One more myth fixes Honshū's western half to the imperial story. When Amaterasu sent her grandson down to take the land, its ruler — Ōkuninushi, the great land-master of Izumo — was first challenged through his sons, each defeated in turn, and then visited by the divine negotiators with a counter-offer: yield the visible world to heaven's line, and in exchange heaven would build him a shrine 'with its pillars thick at the base and high at the head' and house his spirit there ( Kojiki , age of the heavenly grandchild). Ōkuninushi accepted. The Nihon Shoki remembers the bargain as a settled diplomatic exchange — Japan's mythic account of how the western realms joined the Yamato order without a war of conquest. Izumo Taisha, on Honshū's Sea-of-Japan coast, stands where the deal was struck, and the vast pillars its ancient halls once held were, by tradition, exactly the size the god stipulated. The myth is a charter for peaceful annexation: the land yields, the god is honored, and both houses — Izumo's shrine and the imperial palace — stand on the same island.

Tell me a myth about "Gaurī".

Input: Gaurī

Gaurī's myths are the Great Goddess's domestic epic: the mountain-daughter who becomes the universe's mother through patience — Satī reborn, Śiva out-waited, two sons made, and a calendar of festivals that still re-enacts her story in millions of homes. [The Birth] Daughter of the Mountain: The Purāṇas remember her previous body: Satī, daughter of Dakṣa, who burned herself in the sacrificial fire when her father insulted her husband Śiva — and whose scattered limbs became the Śakti-pīṭhas, the goddess's seats of power spread across the subcontinent. Reborn as Pārvatī, daughter of Himavat the mountain-king, she was Gaurī from the first: the golden girl of the peaks, destined from birth for the ash-covered wanderer who had forgotten how to love. Her name is older than her story — in the Ṛgveda gaurī is simply the feminine of gaura , the golden one of the herds — and the Purāṇas' point is that the name waited: the cow-gold of the dawn hymns becomes, in time, the skin of the Mother. The myth means the goddess keeps her bodies the way a lineage keeps its house: burned down and rebuilt, but never homeless. [The Penance] Winning the Unwinnable: When beauty and Kāma's flower-arrows failed to move Śiva in his grief for Satī, she chose tapas : years of austerity in the forest — leaves for food, rain for bath, standing on one leg through the seasons. The Śiva Purāṇa tells the test: Śiva came disguised as a stammering young brahmin and mocked her wasted devotion and her emaciated god; offered instead his own beautiful form; everything but her vow was negotiable, and she would not be dissuaded. Conquered by patience, the ascetic asked for her hand, and the gods gathered at Kailāsa for the wedding the Purāṇas tell as the universe's own — Himavat giving the bride, the Ganges and the moon attending, the mountains dancing. The myth means that in the Śākta world the courtship is reversed: it is the goddess who woos, the god who is won, and the victory belongs to work rather than grace. [The Mother] Two Sons, One Lap: Of her own body she shaped Gaṇeśa — the gatekeeper-son molded from the turmeric-and-sandalwood paste of her skin while she bathed — and of the gods' combined fire came Kārttikeya (Skanda), the war-son she raised as her own. The elephant-headed and the six-faced, the remover of obstacles and the destroyer of demons: both call her Mātā, and the texts make her maternity the point of the household's theology. Her Gaṇeśa story is hers most of all: when the boy barred Śiva from her bath and the gods fell on him, Śiva's stroke took his head — and the goddess's grief, in which the worlds shook, moved the gods to restore him with an elephant's head, the first head that came to hand. A son made without any male, defended by a mother against all heaven: the Purāṇas say her lap is where the world's two busiest gods still rest. The myth means motherhood here is sovereign — the children are made, not granted, and the making is worship. [The Festival] Gaurī Vṛata: Her living myth is the calendar: the Tṛtīyā fasts and the Gaurī festivals of Maharashtra and the South, where married women pray for their households' wellbeing and unmarried girls for good husbands — honoring the goddess who won the ideal marriage by her own effort. The rite is precise: the golden image is made, worshipped, and fed for three days; then it is carried to the river and immersed — the mother received as a daughter and released as a goddess, like a bride returning to her husband's house. In its theology the vrata re-enacts her penance in miniature: the fasting women of the festival perform, for three days, the austerity by which she performed the impossible. The myth means devotion is biography read aloud — her story, told yearly to the next generation of daughters, with turmeric for ink and the household for its page.

Tell me a myth about "Ọbà".

Input: Ọbà

Ọba's myths are domestic tragedy told as hydrology: the co-wife's war that became a river and a lake. The cycle survives in Yoruba oral tradition — oríkì praise-poetry and the folktale corpus recorded by Bascom and others — and crossed the Atlantic to become the diaspora's parable of the polygamous household. [The oral corpus] Three Wives, One Storm: Ṣàngó, the thunder-king, took three river-wives: Ọba the senior, Ọṣun the beloved, and Ọya the storm-sharer. The cycle survives in the oríkì praise-poetry and the folktale corpus recorded by Yoruba specialists from the mid-twentieth century — Wande Abimbola's editions of Ifá verse, William Bascom's collections of tales — and in the diaspora the three wives became the standard cast of every household drama. The tellings agree on the shape: Ọba, the first wife, watched her husband's love flow downhill to Ọṣun, and love that is watched curdles into jealousy. In the fullest tellings Ọba schemed against Ọṣun — and Ọṣun, the shrewdest of the household, let the scheme come to her first and answered it with one that would end the rivalry. The seniority that should have protected Ọba is exactly what the story burns: in the thunder-king's house, the first wife is the last to be believed, and the household's peace is purchased with her humiliation. [The folktale cycle] The Ear in the Soup: The trap is the cycle's most famous scene, preserved in the folktale collections (Bascom, African Folktales) and endlessly retold in the diaspora. Ọṣun — in some tellings Ọya — let fall that the king loved, above all things, the taste of his beloved's ear in his soup. Ọba, desperate to be loved again, cut off her own ear and cooked it for him. When the bowl came before Ṣàngó and the trick stood revealed, his disgust and rage drove her from the palace; the co-wives laughed, and Ọba fled north weeping, her maimed head hidden under her crown and her hair. The sources disagree on which co-wife set the trap and on how much of the truth Ṣàngó ever learned — the oral tradition keeps the variants alive rather than settling them. What every telling keeps is the ear: the organ of obedience, cut off to buy a love that was never for sale. The myth is the Yoruba anatomy of jealousy — not the villain's punishment, but the victim's self-mutilation, and the crown she designed afterward to live with it. [The lake] The Water of Her Grief: Her tears became her realm. In the tellings, Ọba's flight ended in the water that still bears her name: the Ọba River of Yorubaland, and the lake of her worship, where her priests keep her cult and the faithful mourn with her on her appointed days. The geography is the theology — a goddess exiled from the palace takes the river as her palace, and the quiet water outlasts the thunder. The tradition preserves one firm ritual rule from the household war: Ọba and Ọya, the senior wife and the storm-sharer, can never be honored in the same shrine; some quarrels the orisha themselves decline to reconcile. But her people read the ending differently than the palace did: storms pass, the river stays. The senior wife outlasted the storm-god's louder wives by becoming the thing the storm cannot be — permanent, low, and always arriving. [The diaspora] Obá Crosses the Water: The wives' cycle crossed the Middle Passage with the orisha, and in the Americas it acquired its second life. In Cuba's Santería she is Obá, syncretized with Santa Catalina de Alejandría — whose wheel she shares, and whose feast day, 25 November, became hers; her cult proved strongest in Matanzas province, where her initiates arrange the hair forward over the ears exactly as she arranged hers, the gesture intact across four hundred years and an ocean. In Brazil's Candomblé, Obá keeps her river and her covered ear, and the three-wives drama remains the standard parable told to explain the polygamous household's wars and survivors. Robert Farris Thompson documented how thoroughly the diaspora kept her iconography — the hidden ear is legible in Lucumí altars from Havana to Miami. The crossing is itself the last episode of the myth: the wife the palace expelled became the orisha the ocean could not drown, carried in the hair of women who had lost everything else and still arranged it, forward, covering, dignified.

Tell me a myth about "Balor".

Input: Balor

Balor's dossier is short and total: he exists in the tradition to be the thing that must be brought down. Cath Maige Tuired gives him the war's most famous single stroke, the Lebor Gabála fixes his lineage and his wife's vengeance, and the Donegal oral tradition supplies the prophecy, the tower, and the stolen cow that the medieval manuscripts only glance at. The sources disagree on the details and never on the architecture: a gaze that can only destroy, contained at terrible cost, and turned home at last by his own blood. [Lebor Gabála Érenn] Balor Son of Dot, Grandson of Nét: The book of invasions fixes Balor's place before it tells his deeds: Balor mac Doit meic Néit, 'Balor son of Dot, grandson of Nét', king of the Fomorians — the sea-going race who had pressed on Ireland since the age of the Nemedians, exacting tribute from the outer islands. His wife was Cethlenn of the crooked teeth, whose spear struck the Dagda at Mag Tuired; the Lebor Gabála records that the All-Father afterwards died of Cethlenn's wound — the settled price of Balor's war, long counted in the tally of the battle. His daughter was Ethniu, and by Cian — in the Lebor Gabála's genealogy the son of the healer Dian Cécht — she bore Lugh, the Samildánach, equally skilled in all the arts. Thus the Fomorian king was the grandfather of the Túatha Dé Danann's deliverer: the genealogy on which the whole tragedy of Mag Tuired turns, and the reason no tower, sea, or tax could keep the grandson away. [Cath Maige Tuired] How the Eye Was Poisoned: Cath Maige Tuired explains the weapon before it uses it. Balor had a destructive eye, never opened except on a battlefield, and four men were needed to raise its lid with a polished handle that passed through it; any army that eye looked upon was made worthless, though it were many thousands strong. The poison had a childhood. When Balor was a boy, his father's druids were brewing a charm, and the boy looked in on the work; the fumes of the brew rose and struck the eye, and from that day its gaze was venom. The detail is the tradition's whole theory of the figure in one image: power taken in unguarded, as a child takes in smoke, and carried incurably for a lifetime. What entered by accident becomes the foundation of a tyranny — and a tyranny that must hire four men to open its own weapon has already told you how it will end. [The Oral Tradition (Tory Island)] The Tower and the Prophecy: The manuscripts agree that Ethniu was Balor's daughter and Lugh's mother; how that came to be is told by the oral tradition of the north-west, collected in the nineteenth century on and around Tory Island — Balor's sea-girt fortress off the Donegal coast. A druid foretold that Balor would die by the hand of his own grandson, and the king answered the prophecy with masonry: he locked his daughter Eithne in a tower on the rock, with twelve matrons to keep every man from her sight. The doom came in by the door the theft opened. Balor coveted the Glas Gaibhnenn, the grey-green cow of Cian, and stole her across the water; Cian crossed to Tory for redress, and with the druidess Biróg's aid won into the tower in woman's dress and to Eithne's side. When the child was born Balor had him cast into the sea — but the sea gave him back, fostered and hidden, until a young stranger came to Nuadu's court at Tara and was asked what art he practiced. The question the Fomorians could not answer had been growing up under their own doom all along. [Cath Maige Tuired] The Sling-Stone at Mag Tuired: At the second battle of Mag Tuired the armies broke each other all day, and then Balor came against the Túatha Dé Danann with the Fomorian host, destroying and slaughtering. He commanded that the lid of his eye be raised, so that he might blast the enemy with its look — and the four men set the polished handle to the lid. It was then that Lugh cast a sling-stone at him, which carried the eye backward through his head, so that it was his own host that looked into it. Balor fell on top of the Fomorian fighting-men, and twenty-seven of them died beneath his side. The weapon the Fomorians had built their tyranny on spent its last gaze on its owners — and the battle turned with the eye. The Túatha Dé Danann took back the tribute from the defeated host, and the power of the Fomorians over Ireland was broken for good. A gaze made to wither enemies had met the one thing it could not wither: a small stone, aimed.

Tell me a myth about "Helénē".

Input: Helénē

Helénē's story is told by Homer, Hesiod, Stesichorus, Euripides, and Herodotus — and the tradition argues with itself at every turn: abduction or seduction, guilt or phantom, goddess or woman. She is the most examined face in Greek myth. [The Birth] Leda and the Swan: Zeus desired Leda, the wife of King Tyndareus of Sparta, and came to her in the shape of a swan — fleeing, in the usual telling, an eagle's pursuit, so that the queen received the god under her wing. From her egg, and from a second egg, came the mixed brood of the house of Tyndareus: Helénē and her sister Clytemnestra, and the twins Kastor and Polydeukes, the Dioscuri — only some of them children of Zeus, the tradition says, though which is disputed. The earliest witness is Hesiod's Catalogue of Women (fr. 23a M-W), and Euripides opens his Helen with Leda finding the egg and hatching the child within. Aeschylus' Agamemnon (1455ff.) remembers the swan as a bird that sang for its death. The myth gives Helen a double nature from the first breath: born of a god's disguise and a mortal's bed, sister of the saviors of sailors and of the woman who would murder a king. Beauty, the story says, is never simply born — it arrives already entangled with power. [The Suitors] The Oath of Tyndareus: So renowned was Helen's beauty that suitors came to Sparta from every Greek land — and so dangerous was their number that King Tyndareus feared bloodshed whoever won. Odysseus, himself a suitor in some tellings but wise beyond courtship, proposed the oath that bears the king's name: each suitor swore to defend the marriage-rights of the chosen man, with arms if necessary. Then Helen chose Menelaus, brother of Agamemnon, and the oath bound all of Greece to her marriage. The story is preserved in Hesiod's Catalogue (fr. 198 M-W) and in the Cypria tradition; Homer has Helen on the walls of Troy look down at the Achaean champions and ask, without irony, whom they have left at home for her sake ( Iliad 3.205-224). The oath converts a wedding into a treaty — and a treaty, as the next generation would learn, is only a war waiting for its pretext. [The Judgment] The Apple of the Fairest: When Paris, prince of Troy, was asked to award a golden apple inscribed 'to the fairest,' he chose Aphrodite, who promised him the most beautiful woman alive — Helen, then Menelaus' wife. What followed depends on whom you read. The Cypria tradition (Proclus' summary) makes Paris a guest in Menelaus' house who sails off with the queen while her husband is away in Crete; the Iliad says only that Hera, Athena, and Aphrodite 'came to the shepherd's valley' and that the goddess led her away ( Iliad 24.25-30); Stesichorus and Herodotus insist she never went at all, carried off to Egypt while a phantom burned Troy in her shape. Homer himself refuses to settle it: Helen in the Odyssey (4.261-264) says Aphrodite 'cast in my heart sweet longing' and drove her from her marriage-bed. Abduction, seduction, or frame — the sources disagree, and the disagreement is the myth: an entire war needed a cause, and Greece could never quite decide what Helen's part had been. [At Troy] The Woman on the Walls: Ten years in Troy, and Helénē becomes the war's most unsettled witness. In Iliad 3 she walks the wall with Priam, naming the Greek champions — Agamemnon, Odysseus, Aias, and her own brothers, whom a mist strangely prevents her from seeing. The old king, whose city is dying for her, calls her 'dear child' and refuses blame: 'for my part, I hold the gods responsible' (3.164-165). She watches Menelaus and Paris duel for her, and shudders at Aphrodite's unseen hand when the goddess spirits her stricken husband from the field. And in Iliad 6 she is found at her loom, weaving the battles of Trojans and Achaeans into a purple web — a woman archiving a war fought in her name, while Hector, gentlest of the princes, calls her 'sister' and asks only to be remembered. Homer gives Helen what later retellings often withhold: full consciousness . She is the first to blame herself — 'dog that I am' — in a poem that pointedly refuses to. [The Return] The Phantom and Egypt: How Helen ended the war is disputed; how she came home is, too. Stesichorus of Himera paid the price of telling her story 'wrong' — legend says he went blind — and recanted in the Palinode , preserved in Plato's Phaedrus (243a): 'that story is not true; you never went in the benched ships, nor came to the towers of Troy.' Herodotus (2.112-120), told the same by Egyptian priests, locates the real Helen in the palace of the shape-shifting sea-old man Proteus at Memphis, while a phantom went to Troy. Homer offers the peaceful third act: in Odyssey 4, Telemachus finds Helen and Menelaus at home in Sparta, magnificently reconciled, she dropping the drug nepenthe into the wine to make grief forgetful. Three endings — phantom, hostage, homecoming — and each lets her live. The tradition, unable to convict or acquit her, instead multiplied her until no single Helen could be condemned.

Tell me a myth about "Mārs".

Input: Mārs

Mārs enters myth almost entirely as a father — and what he fathers is the city. His stories are told by Rome's historians, not by its Homer, and they all serve one thesis: that Roman power is divine in origin and therefore answerable to ritual . The Vestal and the she-wolf, the shield from heaven, the old king fooled at a wedding: each myth is a charter for a piece of the state cult. [The Vestal and the Twins] Rhea Silvia at the River: Livy opens the Roman story with a vestal crime that is really a divine plan (1.3–4). Numitor, rightful king of Alba Longa, is deposed by his brother Amulius, who forces Numitor's daughter, the Vestal Rhea Silvia, into perpetual virginity so the line cannot challenge him. But the girl, sent to fetch water for a sacrifice, is overpowered in the sacred grove by the god — or so she swears, 'by the god himself, she said that Mars was the author of her seized virginity' — and bears twin boys. Amulius orders them drowned in the Tiber; the river is in flood, the basket grounds at the fig-tree Ruminalis, and a she-wolf comes down from the hills to nurse them in the cave of the Lupercal, while a woodpecker flies food to the infants. The shepherd Faustulus finds them; his wife Acca Larentia raises them; and the twins grow up to restore Numitor and found a city of their own on the Palatine. Livy reports the whole wonder-story and then, with the honesty that makes him Rome's first historian, adds that he gives it as it has come down, 'more adorned with poetry than burdened by proof.' The myth needs no proof: it explains why the war god's temple stands at the heart of the city his sons built. [The Shield from Heaven] Numa and the Ancile: In Numa's peaceful reign — the king who talked Jupiter himself out of human sacrifice with a handful of meal and onions — a shield fell from the sky, the ancile, with a promise that Rome's fate hung upon it. The problem was theft: one true shield, an empire to protect, and every enemy a potential thief. So the king set the cunning smith Mamurius Veturius a test he could not be told about — make eleven copies so exact that even Numa could not pick the divine original — and the twelve ancilia were entrusted to the Salii, the 'leapers,' priests of Mars who danced through the city each March bearing the shields on their left arms and singing a carmen so ancient that even Augustus's scholars confessed they could barely construe it. The smith who made them was driven out, or stoned, or honored — the versions disagree, and Ovid is visibly embarrassed by the tradition — but the ancilia stayed, and were still being carried when the empire was Christian. Mars's shield, like Rome itself, was a copy indistinguishable from the original; that was the whole point. [The Avenger] The Vow at Philippi: The greatest Mars myth is not archaic at all — it is Augustan, and paid for in blood. After Caesar's murder the nineteen-year-old Octavian marched with Antony against the Liberatores, and at Philippi in 42 BC Brutus and Cassius fell, one by the sword, one by his own hand. Octavian had vowed a temple to Mars the Avenger — Mars Ultor — if he should win, and forty years later, in 2 BC, he dedicated it in his new Forum, flanked by colossal statues of the god in crested helmet, spear grounded, breastplate crowded with myth. The temple held the sword of the murdered Caesar and the standards recovered from the Parthians — Crassus's lost eagles finally retrieved by diplomacy and displayed as war won. Ovid, who was there, makes the dedication Rome's birthday party (Fasti 5.545–598): the new theater, the games, the imperial family on the podium, and Mars's godhead finally visible — for until the temple rose, the Romans admitted, no image of Mars had any reliable claim to show what the god looked like. The myth is exactly as blunt as its name: the man who avenged the father became the son of a god, and Mars was the instrument. [The Old King Fooled] Mars and Anna Perenna: Ovid is the only source, and he is delighted to be it (Fasti 3.523–710). Old Mars, he says, had fallen in love — with the warlike maiden Ana Perenna? No: with Minerva herself, who with a goddess's perfect tact referred him onward: 'you are old; she is young' — go woo Anna, 'the years' own goddess.' Anna knew what the old god was after and, on their wedding night, wrapped herself in a veil, went to the bedroom in the dark, and — had placed the aged crone in the bed instead. When Mars at last lifted the veil by the lamp's light, the laugh was heard all over heaven, and Anna was raised to the skies as the river of years. The story is the Fasti's gift to Mars: the most ferocious of the gods made ridiculous by age and desire, and answered not with thunder but with a practical joke — Roman humor at the war god's expense, told in the month of his festival. [The Enemy of Aeneas] Mars for Turnus: In Virgil's Aeneid Mars does for the losing side what he never does for Rome: he loves it. His favorite is Turnus, the Rutulian prince who defends Italy against the Trojan landing, and the god moves through the last books like a pressure behind the war: he sends Allecto, the Fury, to kindle the conflict in Book 7; he strikes Turnus with a courage beyond his own when the prince pursues a phantom Aeneas onto a ship and is carried helpless from the field in Book 9; and in Book 12, when the treaty breaks, Mars arms him for the last duel. Yet Jupiter has already weighed the fates, and not even the war god's advocacy moves the scale. Mars rages; fate is silent and exact. The scene is the Aeneid's quiet commentary on the god Rome trusted most: Mars can arm a hero, but he cannot assign the victory — and when Rome itself is at stake, the poet reminds us, the god of war fights on the other side too.

Tell me a myth about "Medb".

Input: Medb

Medb's dossier is the Táin Bó Cúailnge, the longest and greatest tale of the Ulster Cycle — and unlike every other great name in Irish myth, she is not a goddess remembered as a woman but a queen the tradition may once have worshipped as a goddess. The tale itself never says which. [Táin Bó Cúailnge, Recension I] The Pillow-Talk: One night at Crúachan, when the royal bed had been made for Medb and Ailill, they fell into a 'bolster-conversation' — comrac chind cherchailli — and Ailill boasted that the woman married to a wealthy man is well off. Medb answered that she was well off before him: daughter of Eochu Feidlech, high king of Ireland, and the wealthier of the two. To settle it they had every treasure counted — cups, rings, cattle, sheep, horses — and the tally came out exactly even, save one item: the great bull Finnbennach, born in Medb's herd, had scorned to be counted a woman's chattel and walked over into Ailill's, where he stood as the White-Horned of Connacht. That one beast broke the equality Medb would not live without. Her steward Mac Roth found the match: the Donn of Cúailnge, the Brown Bull of Cooley, kept by Dáire mac Fiachna in Ulster. Medb sent for a year's loan of him at princely terms — fifty heifers a year, a stretch of the plain of Aí, her own chariot, and the friendship of her thighs — and Dáire agreed. But the messengers drank and boasted that had the loan been refused they would have taken the bull by force, and Dáire swore that only by force would he ever be taken. The embassy came home empty, and Medb resolved on war. [Táin Bó Cúailnge, Recension I] The Bride-Gift Speech: The Táin lets Medb state her own terms, and the speech is the charter of her queenship. Daughter of the high king, wooed by the kings of Ireland, she refused them all, she says, 'for I asked a strange bride-gift such as no woman before me had asked of a man of the men of Ireland — a husband without meanness, without jealousy, without fear.' If he were mean, their wealth could not sit together, for she is generous in gifts; if jealous, she could not live beside him, 'for I was never without one man in the shadow of another'; if fearful, he would shame her in the front of every fight. Such a man she found in Ailill mac Máta: no meanness, no jealousy, no fear. She brought him the bride-gift — the clothing of twelve men, a chariot worth thrice seven cumals, the width of his face in red gold, the weight of his left forearm in bronze — and it is into her province, not his, that he came. The Táin is blunt about the arithmetic: he is king of Connacht because he is married to Medb of Crúachan. [Táin Bó Cúailnge] The Debility and the Boy at the Ford: Medb timed the raid for the cess noínden, the pangs of the Ulstermen — the debility laid on the warriors of Ulster by [[macha|Macha]], whom they had forced to race the king's horses when she was great with child. With Ulster's fighting-men abed, Medb marched the hosting of four provinces north — Connacht's own, the Leinster Galeóin, and the exiles of Ulster under Fergus mac Róich, who knew every road and ford of the way and, the tale says plainly, shared the queen's bed with Ailill's leave, for the road could not be found without him. One boy stood against the whole hosting: [[cuchulainn|Cú Chulainn]], untouched by the debility, who held the fords in single combat and took the heads of the best of Connacht one by one. Medb spent everything on him — terms, ambushes, satirists, her daughter Findabair promised to a dozen champions at once — and the hardest price fell on Ferdia, Cú Chulainn's own foster-brother, whom she plied with drink and the promise of Findabair until he took the ford. Four days they fought; the gae bolga ended it; and the march went on over the body of the one man Medb could not buy twice. [Táin Bó Cúailnge] The Battle of the Bulls: The hosts met at Gáirech and Irgáirech when the pangs lifted and Ulster rose; Medb's army broke, but the prize was already driven south — she had the Donn of Cúailnge, and she covered the retreat herself, in the tale's most unsparing passage, when her gush of blood came on her and she asked Cú Chulainn's protection for her army's rear. He granted it: 'no coward's weapon is the weapon of a woman.' Fergus mac Róich, looking back over the ruin of the hosting, gave the raid its verdict: 'This is what usually happens to a herd of horses led by a mare — their substance is taken and carried off and destroyed as they follow a woman who has misled them.' The bulls settled the account themselves. Finnbennach saw the Donn and bellowed; they fought through the night across Ireland, and in the morning the men of Connacht found the Brown Bull standing over the White-Horned trampled to pieces. The Donn carried Finnbennach's carcass on his horns through Connacht — scattering the loin at Áth Luain, the liver at Trim — then turned north for Cúailnge and died there of his wounds and his victory. Medb had her bull, and her equality, and the Táin's dry arithmetic: the two most valuable beasts in Ireland, both dead, and nothing left to count. [Aided Meidbe] The Cheese of Inis Cloithrinn: Medb outlived the raid, outlived Ailill — slain at Conall Cernach's hand — and kept her sovereignty into age, spending her last years at Inis Cloithrinn, her island on Lough Ree, where she bathed in the pool every morning at sunrise. She had killed her sister Clothru, and Clothru's son Furbaide had been cut from his mother's womb — whence his name, Ferbend, 'of the cutting' — and he grew up with the debt of it. Furbaide found the queen's bathing place and measured it the patient way: morning after morning he stood on the shore opposite and practiced his cast against the distance, until the stone flew true by habit. Then one sunrise, as Medb came to her bath, his sling let fly — a ball of hard cheese, the tale insists, the humblest weapon in Ireland — and the queen of Connacht, who had moved four provinces against Ulster and asked no man's leave for anything in her life, died by her nephew's hand at the water's edge. Her grave, the local tradition says, is the great cairn on Knocknarea in Sligo, where she stands buried upright, facing Ulster.

Tell me a myth about "Sigurðr".

Input: Sigurðr

Sigurðr is the dragonslayer of the Vǫlsunga cycle, the Norse original of the German Siegfried and the last great hero of the legendary North. Son of Sigmundr and Hjǫrdís, fostered by the smith Reginn, he reforged his father's sword, killed the dragon Fáfnir, and woke the valkyrie Brynhildr from her enchanted sleep — then lost her, and his life, to a draught of forgetfulness and the plotting of his sworn brothers. His story survives in the Poetic Edda, the Prose Edda, and Vǫlsunga saga, and through the Middle High German Nibelungenlied it became the backbone of Wagner's Ring. Where the gods of the Edda face a doom they know is coming, Sigurðr faces one he has forgotten — and that is the more human tragedy. [Vǫlsunga saga] The Reforging of Gramr: At the wedding feast of his sister Signý, a one-eyed stranger — Óðinn — thrust a sword to the hilt into the tree Barnstokkr that grew through the hall of Vǫlsungr, and only Sigmundr of all the company could draw it. Years later Sigmundr fell in battle, the sword shattering beneath him against the same god's spear, and his widow Hjǫrdís carried the shards away for her unborn son. That son, Sigurðr, was fostered by Reginn, a smith of the dwarf-kin, who urged him against the dragon Fáfnir and forged blade after blade that broke under the boy's testing — until Sigurðr demanded the shards of his father's sword be worked into the new steel. Reginn reforged them into Gramr , and the boy clove the smith's anvil to the stock and sheared a tuft of wool drifting on the current as though it were standing stone (Vǫlsunga saga 13–15; Reginsmál). The blade binds the hero to Óðinn from birth: the god who gave the sword also broke it, and the steel that passes from father to son is the visible thread of a destiny the boy never chose. In the North, inheritance is not property but appointment. [Fáfnismál] The Slaying of Fáfnir: Fáfnir was Reginn's brother, who had killed their father Hreiðmarr for the hoard paid as weregild for the slain Ótr, and crawled away to Gnitaheiðr, where greed long brooding over gold twisted him into a dragon. Guided by a one-eyed old man who would not give his name, Sigurðr dug a trench across the worm's path to the water and lay in it; when Fáfnir crawled overhead he thrust Gramr upward into the heart. The dying dragon warned him that the gold would be his death, and the hero answered with the northern creed: every man must die, and wealth must serve until that day (Fáfnismál; Vǫlsunga saga 18–20). Roasting the heart for Reginn, Sigurðr burned his finger, set it in his mouth, and the heart-blood opened the speech of birds to him: the nuthatches in the branches warned that the smith meant to kill him. He took Reginn's head, loaded the cursed gold onto Grani, and rode away the richest and most doomed man in the North. The birds that save him here will not be there at the end. The episode's point is exact: the monster's death transfers the monster's curse, and every new owner of the gold only inherits it. [Sigrdrífumál] The Flame-Wall on Hindarfjall: Before the dragon, on Hindarfjall, Sigurðr found the vafrlogi — a wall of flame no horse would cross — and within it a hall where a warrior slept in full armor, as if dead. The sleep-thorn in her corslet marked her as a valkyrie; he drew Gramr and cut the armor from her, and she woke as Brynhildr and taught him the runes and the lore of the worlds: the healing runes, the ale-runes, the speech of victory and the speech of weddings, and the caution that shapes the whole cycle — never to swear falsely (Sigrdrífumál; Vǫlsunga saga 21–22). They plighted their troth and parted, and she prophesied what he would forget. The flame-wall is the cycle's question about fate: it parts for the destined rider and for no one else, and the man it admits is not thereby saved from what comes after. [Guðrúnarkviða] The Ale of Forgetfulness: At the court of Gjúki's sons the queen Grímhildr brewed Sigurðr the ale of forgetfulness, and Brynhildr passed from his mind as if she had never been. He married Guðrún, swore oaths with her brothers Gunnarr and Hǫgni, and when Gunnarr wooed Brynhildr and could not cross the flames, Sigurðr exchanged shapes with him and rode the fire in his friend's likeness — wooing his own forgotten beloved for another man, with a drawn sword laid between them in the bridal bed (Vǫlsunga saga 28; Guðrúnarkviða I). The deception could not hold: from a ring and a quarrel at the washing-stones Brynhildr learned what had been done, and wounded in her pride she demanded the death of the man who had ridden the flames and then married another. The betrayal is the cycle's quiet engine: no one in it acts from malice until the ale is brewed — the draught of forgetfulness is the one weapon the curse of gold did not need to supply. [Brot af Sigurðarkviðu] The Death of Sigurðr: The brothers, bound to Sigurðr by oath, could not strike him; they incited the younger Guthormr, who had sworn nothing, and he stabbed Sigurðr as he slept. Some lays — Sigurðarkviða en skamma and Guðrún's own laments — have him slain out of doors, in the forest; Brot af Sigurðarkviðu , preserved only in a fragment around the Codex Regius lacuna, gives the death in bed and the last words. Dying, Sigurðr spoke gently to Guðrún, named the true traitors, and flung Gramr after the killers; the sword caught Guthormr in the doorway and took him too. Brynhildr laughed once at the bier, told the truth at last, and went onto the pyre to lie beside him (Sigurðarkviða en skamma; Vǫlsunga saga 31–32). The sources disagree on the place but not on the meaning: the hoard's curse reached the man who thought himself above it, through the only door he had left open — the trust of those he called his own.

Tell me a myth about "Keraunós".

Input: Keraunós

The keraunós is not merely a weapon but the emblem of Zeus's rule — forged at the beginning of his reign, decisive in his two great wars, and terrible against mortals who reach too high or are loved too much. [The Forging] The Cyclopes Arm Zeus: When Zeus came of age to challenge Kronos, Gaiä named his allies: the Cyclopes, one-eyed smiths imprisoned in the depths. Zeus freed them, and they repaid him with the three weapons of heaven — thunder, lightning, and 'the glowing thunderbolt' (Hesiod, Theogony 501–506); the same passage remembers their earlier craft, arms for the gods at the beginning (Theogony 139–141). The bolt is thus born at the exact moment Zeus's power needs a form: before it he is a younger god with grievances, after it he is the storm. Homer never forgets the connection, and calls the bolt simply the weapon when Zeus arms himself at the brink of the Trojan War (Iliad 8.75). The myth explains why no one else may hold it: the keraunós is the signature of sovereignty, forged once and never re-made. [The Titanomachy] Breaking the Old Order: The war between the Olympians and the Titans lasted ten years with no advantage on either side, until Zeus brought up the Cyclopes' gifts. Then heaven changed hands: 'from Olympus he hurled his bolts in succession, and the earth groaned, burning, and the great forests crackled on every side; the whole earth boiled, and the streams of Ocean, and the unharvested sea' (Hesiod, Theogony 687–713). The Titans were struck down, bound, and cast into misty Tartarus behind gates of bronze. The keraunós here is not one throw but a barrage — the first use of concentrated, overwhelming force in Greek myth, and the poem's theological argument that raw elder power yields to armed, organized thunder. Every later bolt-throw reenacts this one: order established by a weapon that cannot be answered, and therefore never has to be. [Typhon] The Bolt Against the Storm-Giant: The last challenger was Typhon, a being with a hundred serpent heads, eyes of fire, and voices that were by turns gods', bulls', and lions'. The whole cosmos recoiled; Zeus met him with the full armory — thunder and lightning first, then 'the thunderbolt, hard and heavy, that casts the blazing light' (Hesiod, Theogony 820–868). The bolt burned the hundred heads, struck Typhon down, and sent him beneath the land, where he still feeds the eruptions of Etna. The combat pairs like with like — storm against storm — and the keraunós wins not by being bigger but by being directed: Typhon is weather without a wielder, the bolt weather that obeys. Greek theology is compressed into the image. Power becomes legitimate only when it serves an ordered hand, and the hand is Zeus's. [Mortals] Semele and Salmoneus: Love and Hubris: Against mortals the bolt keeps two ledgers. Semele, beloved of Zeus and pregnant with Dionysus, was tricked by jealous Hera into asking to see her lover in his full godhead; the promised thunder and lightning destroyed her — though Zeus rescued the unborn child, sewn into his thigh until term (Apollodorus, Library 3.4.3; cf. Homer, Iliad 14.323–325). Salmoneus kept the opposite account: he dragged bronze bridges behind his chariot for thunder and hurled torches for lightning, demanding sacrifices as though he were Zeus; the true keraunós answered and burned him and his city (Apollodorus 1.9.7; Virgil, Aeneid 6.585–594). One mortal died for loving the storm too much, the other for impersonating it. Between them the bolt defines its narrow path: humanity must neither seize divine fire nor counterfeit it — and the keraunós, which never misses, is the eternal enforcer of that narrowness.

Tell me a myth about "Susanō".

Input: Susanō

Susanoo's cycle in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki runs from cosmic vandal to culture hero: expelled from heaven, he conquers the dragon of chaos and founds a kingdom in song — the most humanly told arc of any Japanese deity. [The Birth] From the Nose of Izanagi: When Izanagi purified himself after his flight from Yomi, Amaterasu was born from his left eye and Tsukuyomi from his right; from his nose came Susanoo , whose name the Kojiki writes 須佐之男 and glosses as the swift, impetuous male deity. Izanagi charged him with rule of the sea. But Susanoo never ceased weeping for his dead mother, crying so hard that the mountains withered and the rivers dried. Exasperated, Izanagi expelled him: 'If that is your wish, go to the land of your mother, then' (Kojiki 1). The storm god is thus the grieving child of creation, defined from birth by a longing for what cannot be retrieved — the sea he was given to rule is, after all, the element his father had fled into to escape death. [The Rampage] The Test and the Trampling: Climbing to heaven to bid his sister farewell, Susanoo alarmed Amaterasu, who went out armed; he protested his innocence and proposed an ukei , a covenant of sincerity, exchanging ornaments so that she bore three goddesses from his sword and he five gods from her necklace (Kojiki 1). The test cleared him — and he repaid it by trampling down the ridges of her rice-fields, filling the ditches, and flaying the heavenly piebald horse, whose carcass he hurled through the roof of her weaving hall, killing the maiden within. Amaterasu fled into the rock cave and sealed the door. Every one of his crimes strikes at cultivation — field, ditch, loom — the arts by which heaven imposes order on nature. Susanoo's rage is the sacred vandalism of the untamed. [The Serpent] The Eight-Forked Monster of Izumo: Banned from heaven, Susanoo descended to Izumo, where he found the old couple Ashinazuchi and Tenazuchi weeping beside their eighth daughter: each year the serpent Yamata no Orochi — eight heads, eight tails, cedars growing on its back, its body spanning eight valleys — had devoured one of their daughters, and Kushinadahime alone remained. Susanoo transformed the girl into a comb, hid her in his hair, and had the parents brew eight vats of eightfold-refined sake. The serpent drank all eight, fell into a stupor, and Susanoo cut it apart (Kojiki 1). In its tail his blade struck something hard: a great sword, which he named Ame-no-Murakumo , Gathering-of-Clouds, and presented to Amaterasu in atonement — the blade later generations call Kusanagi , one of the Three Imperial Regalia. The myth tames chaos not by greater force but by appetite itself: the monster is destroyed by the one thing it could not refuse. [The Palace] Suga, Where the Clouds Rise: After the slaying, Susanoo felt his spirit suddenly clear — suga , refreshed — and on that spot in Izumo he built a palace and married Kushinadahime. Pacing its length, he composed what the Kojiki presents as his own song: 'The many-fenced palace of Suga, ah! That cloud-rising, many-fenced palace of mine!' — counted among the earliest verses in the chronicle and remembered as the foundation of Izumo's sacred landscape. The shrine that marks the site, Suga Jinja, still stands within the orbit of the Izumo tradition, and the verse he sang there is counted among the oldest human voices in Japanese literature. The storm god, having destroyed heaven's order, founds his own in song and marriage: violence converts to culture at the moment it ceases to rage — and the proof is a poem, not a sword. [The Wanderer] The Lodging at Somin's House: The Nihon Shoki adds a stranger chapter. Expelled and unkempt, Susanoo wandered as a beggar and asked lodging of two brothers: the wealthy one refused him, but the poor Somin Shōrai bathed him with sake in eight tubs and fed him well. In gratitude the god gave Somin a charm cut from a mulberry bough: hang this at your gate, and pestilence will pass your house by. The promise held, and the Somin charm became the ancestor of the epidemic-warding talisman-papers hung at gates in Kyōto and across Japan — the same charm-papers still distributed at the Gion cult's shrines today. Behind the terror of the storm stands an old cultic logic: the dangerous god is also the god who protects, and his protection is won by generosity to the stranger at the door.

Tell me a myth about "Oidípous".

Input: Oidípous

Oidípous is the subject of the most perfectly constructed tragedy in the Greek corpus. Homer, Hesiod and Pindar preserve fragments of his story; Sophocles gave it its final form in two plays set forty years apart — one the anatomy of self-discovery, the other the redemption of the polluted man. His fate is never a secret: the audience knows it from the first line, and that is the point. [The Exposure] Pinned Ankles on Kithairon: Laios, king of Thebes, was warned by the Delphic oracle that the son born to him would kill his father. When the child came, he ordered it exposed on Mount Kithairon with a pin driven through its ankles to fix it to the ground; a shepherd took pity and passed the baby to a Corinthian, who carried it to the childless king Polybos. The wound named the child — Oidípous, ‘Swollen-foot’ — and the name told the story to every Greek who heard it. Homer already knows the tale in outline (Odyssey 11.271–280), Pindar tells how Laios, ‘who met the glorious oracle’, was destroyed by the son he feared (Olympian 2.35–42), and Sophocles keeps the pins (Oidipous Tyrannos 1034–1046). The myth's engine is visible from the first scene: every act of prevention is a further link in the chain. The shepherd's pity — the one merciful gesture in the story — is exactly the mechanism by which the oracle is armed. [The Riddle] The Singer at the Gates: On his road to Thebes Oidípous met the Sphinx — ‘who plagued the Cadmeans’, as Hesiod calls her, the daughter of Typhon and Echidna (Theogony 326–329) — and she put the riddle: what creature walks on four legs at dawn, two at noon and three in the evening. Citizens of Thebes had died for failing it; Oidípous answered man , who crawls, walks upright and leans on a staff in old age, and the Sphinx threw herself down from her rock. Grateful Thebes gave him the vacant throne and the widowed queen Jocasta. Sophocles has him tell it plainly: the man who saved the city by answering a question about the human condition could not ask the question that mattered about himself (OT 391–402). The riddle is the tragedy in miniature. He solved the case of humanity in general and failed his own — and the two failures are one failure, of self-knowledge. [The Revelation] The Hour of Truth: Years later a plague fell on Thebes, and the oracle answered: drive out the killer of Laios. Oidípous, now king, swore to find him. Tiresias named the king himself and was dismissed in rage; the testimony of the survivor of Laios' party, then of the old shepherd who had received the exposed infant, closed the circuit piece by piece. Jocasta understood first and hanged herself; Oidípous, raging through the palace, took the golden brooches from her dress and put out his own eyes, so as never again to see what he had done (Sophocles, OT 1146–1297). Homer preserves an older variant in which the queen — there called Epicaste — hangs herself and the gods at once make the whole thing known, yet Oidipous ‘endured’ and continued to rule in Thebes (Odyssey 11.271–280): the tradition itself is of two minds about what the knowledge costs. Sophocles' version is the one the world kept, because it stages the structure of self-discovery exactly: the answer is known from the start to everyone except the one man who most needs it, and recognition, not the deed, is the drama. [The Exile] The Blind King at Colonus: The blinded king went into exile led by his daughter Antigone, a beggar and a holy terror, until he came to the grove of the Eumenides at Colonus, Sophocles' own village. There, as a suppliant of the dread goddesses, he begged Theseus for protection; he withstood Creon, who came to drag him back to Thebes, and received with tears the prayer of his son Polyneices — whom he then cursed. Thunder sounded, the grove filled with voices, and Oidípous walked unguided into the secret place of the goddesses and was seen no more; Theseus alone was permitted to know where a mortal may not go (Sophocles, Oidipous at Colonus 84–110, 1518–1666). The polluted man becomes a source of blessing, and the outcast a guardian power: Sophocles, an old man writing as Athenian fortunes collapsed, gave the exile a holy and politically precious death — and the play ends where his own ashes lie. [The House] The Curse on the Sons: The curse Oidípous pronounced at Colonus — that his sons should divide their inheritance with the sword — fell exactly as spoken. Polyneices, exiled by his brother Eteocles, brought the Seven against Thebes; the brothers killed each other before the walls, and the war of the aftermath came for the daughters: Antigone buried Polyneices against Creon's edict and died for it. Aeschylus had already staged the fatal duel in the Seven Against Thebes, and the epic cycle told the whole descent. The curse is the myth's final demonstration of its law: the hero's story is not an event but a house, and what the oracle begins, the second generation completes. That is why the name outgrew the man: Oidípous names not a deed but a structure — the way inherited guilt passes down a family line until nothing is left to carry it.

Input: Yùhuáng

The Jade Emperor's mythology is a late, literate construction — scripture, novel, and folk tale jointly building a biography and a government for Heaven. His stories ask the great bureaucratic question: who, exactly, is in charge? The answer, assembled from the fifth century to the Ming novel, is a sovereign with a résumé, a war record, and a court that even comedy cannot overthrow. [Yuhuang benxing jijing] The Making of a Sovereign: The Daoist canon answers the obvious question — where does Heaven's emperor come from? — with a full sacred biography. The Scripture of the Jade Sovereign's Former Deeds (Gaoshang Yuhuang benxing jijing, in the Ming Daozang) tells of the childless king of the Kingdom of Wondrous Bliss, whose queen, after years of prayer to the Dao, dreams that the supreme Lord hands her an infant wrapped in radiance. The prince, grown, marvels that even his happy kingdom cannot spare him from death; he gives the throne to a worthy minister and withdraws to the mountain to cultivate the Way — through kalpas of austerity, service to prior immortals, and ordeal after ordeal, until he ascends as Yùhuáng, the Jade Sovereign of the clearest heaven. The scripture thus gives the celestial throne a curriculum vitae: Heaven's ruler is not born but made, refined like an alchemist's elixir across ages no chronicle can hold. [Benxing jijing · Popular Canon] The War Against the Demon Host: The same scripture and the popular tradition that grew from it give the future emperor his proving war. While the radiant prince still rules in his father's kingdom, a demon king — lord of black clouds, master of hosts — brings plague and darkness upon the world, and the gods of the older heavens cannot end him. The prince arms himself, and in the great battle that follows his radiance alone routs the demon armies; the defeated host swears fealty, and the victor — refusing even the throne of the conquered — returns to his mountain and his cultivation. Later novels, above all the Ming Investiture of the Gods (Fengshen yanyi), pour the same pattern over heaven itself, where the mandate passes from defeated tyrants to a righteous successor. The myth's grammar is that of every dynastic founding: the old order falls not because the gods fail, but because the throne must change hands before its holder can be seen at all. [Journey to the West, chs. 3–7] The Monkey and the Throne: In chapters 3–7 of the Ming novel Journey to the West, the Jade Emperor's heaven is the most vividly drawn bureaucracy in Chinese literature. When the stone-born monkey Sun Wukong arms himself in the dragon palace and erases his name from the registers of death, the celestial court debates: execute him or enroll him? He is enrolled — as Bimawen, a groom of heavenly horses — and when he discovers the rank is beneath his power, his rebellion lays open the whole military establishment: the pagoda-bearing general Li Jing, the thunder agents, the star officers all give way, until the Jade Emperor's own high ministers advise the one move left, and the Buddha comes. The episode is comic, but its seriousness is structural: the Emperor of Heaven rules through precedent, rank, and memorial — and comedy is what happens when raw force meets paperwork that cannot imagine it. [Folk Tradition] The Decree Above the Milky Way: In the oldest tellings of the Cowherd and the Weaver Girl — a love story already glimpsed in the Shijing and given its full shape in Han-dynasty lore — the lovers' separation is the work of Heaven itself; and in the later folk versions it is the Jade Emperor, the Weaver Girl's own grandfather (or the Queen Mother of the West at his side), who draws the River of Heaven between them, decreeing that magpies may span it on the seventh night of the seventh month, and only on that night. The festival of Qixi, still kept across East Asia, is the living calendar of this decree. The myth gives the celestial sovereign his strangest office: he is the authority who separates, and the tenderness of the tale is that his separation is annually, faithfully, and by the whole bird-world, undone.
